Furthermore, we showcase the transferability of our steering vectors across different models/LoRAs and highlight the synergistic benefits of applying multiple vectors simultaneously.

papers.title: Steering Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: In this work, we investigate the potential of Activation Steering, a technique originally developed for controlling text generation in Large Language Models (LLMs), to direct PLMs toward generating protein sequences with targeted properties.
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first application of activation steering to Protein Language Models, enabling property-specific protein generation without retraining, and proposes a novel optimization framework (ASPO) that integrates activation steering with mutation site identification.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering is a viable and powerful paradigm for guiding PLMs to generate and optimize proteins with desired properties, offering a scalable and efficient alternative to traditional methods.
papers.key_findings:
Activation steering effectively guides PLMs to generate protein sequences with enhanced thermostability and solubility, outperforming fine-tuning and original models.
The proposed ASPO framework achieves the highest fitness scores in protein optimization tasks for thermostability, solubility, and GFP brightness.
Activation steering maintains or improves sequence diversity and novelty compared to baselines.
The method is sensitive to the size of positive/negative sets and steering strength, with recommended defaults provided.
Activation steering can simultaneously optimize multiple properties.
papers.abstract: Protein Language Models (PLMs), pre-trained on extensive evolutionary data from natural proteins, have emerged as indispensable tools for protein design. While powerful, PLMs often struggle to produce proteins with precisely specified functionalities or properties due to inherent challenges in controlling their outputs. In this work, we investigate the potential of Activation Steering, a technique originally developed for controlling text generation in Large Language Models (LLMs), to direct PLMs toward generating protein sequences with targeted properties. We propose a simple yet effective method that employs activation editing to steer PLM outputs, and extend this approach to protein optimization through a novel editing site identification module. Through comprehensive experiments on lysozyme-like sequence generation and optimization, we demonstrate that our methods can be seamlessly integrated into both auto-encoding and autoregressive PLMs without requiring additional training. These results highlight a promising direction for precise protein engineering using foundation models.

papers.title: Can sparse autoencoders be used to decompose and interpret steering vectors?
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why directly applying sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two main reasons why sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide misleading decompositions of steering vectors: (1) steering vectors are out-of-distribution for SAEs, and (2) SAEs cannot represent negative coefficients which are meaningful in steering vectors.
papers.conclusion: Direct SAE decomposition of steering vectors is misleading due to out-of-distribution and non-negativity constraints; alternative approaches such as learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors have significantly smaller L2-norms than model activations, causing the SAE encoder bias to dominate the decomposition and yield misleading results.
Scaling steering vectors does not resolve the out-of-distribution issue because steering vectors lack default components present in model activations.
SAEs restrict decompositions to non-negative coefficients, but steering vectors have meaningful negative projections in feature directions.
Negative projections in steering vectors can cause spurious positive activations in SAE features due to negative cosine similarities between features.
These issues explain prior observations of irrelevant features in SAE decompositions and the failure of SAE-reconstructed vectors to retain steering properties.
papers.limitation:
The proposed alternative method of learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis requires two SAE decompositions per difference vector, increasing the potential impact of SAE error.
The corrigibility steering vectors may include confounding features related to computer science and language modeling.
future_direction: Explore learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis and establish evaluation metrics to compare with alternative methods.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a promising approach to control the behaviour of large language models. However, their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) may offer a potential method to interpret steering vectors, recent findings show that SAE-reconstructed vectors often lack the steering properties of the original vectors. This paper investigates why directly applying SAEs to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions, identifying two reasons: (1) steering vectors fall outside the input distribution for which SAEs are designed, and (2) steering vectors can have meaningful negative projections in feature directions, which SAEs are not designed to accommodate. These limitations hinder the direct use of SAEs for interpreting steering vectors.

papers.title: Belief Dynamics Reveal the Dual Nature of In-Context Learning and Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Whether in-context learning and activation steering are instances of a broader framework for controlling LLM behavior, and how they jointly affect model behavior.
papers.core_contribution: Presents a Bayesian belief dynamics model that unifies in-context learning and activation steering, accurately predicting LLM behavior under both interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Bayesian belief dynamics model unifies in-context learning and activation steering, accurately predicting LLM behavior and revealing a phase boundary between interventions.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning and activation steering jointly affect behavior, creating a phase boundary modulated by context and activations.
The Bayesian model predicts sigmoidal learning curves as in-context evidence accumulates and additivity of interventions in log-belief space.
The model predicts crossover points (N*) where behavior transitions between concepts, with high correlation to empirical data.
The linear representation hypothesis holds within a range of steering magnitudes, beyond which behavior breaks down.
The model generalizes across different LLMs (Llama, Gemma, Qwen) and datasets (persona, sentiment).
papers.limitation: The linear representation hypothesis breaks down with large steering magnitudes, leading to chance behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be controlled at inference time through prompts (in-context learning) and internal activations (activation steering). Different accounts have been proposed to explain these methods, yet their common goal of controlling model behavior raises the question of whether these seemingly disparate methodologies can be seen as specific instances of a broader framework. Motivated by this, we develop a unifying, predictive account of LLM control from a Bayesian perspective. Specifically, we posit that both context- and activation-based interventions impact model behavior by altering its belief in latent concepts: steering operates by changing concept priors, while in-context learning leads to an accumulation of evidence. This results in a closed-form Bayesian model that is highly predictive of LLM behavior across context- and activation-based interventions in a set of domains inspired by prior work on many-shot in-context learning. This model helps us explain prior empirical phenomena - e.g., sigmoidal learning curves as in-context evidence accumulates - while predicting novel ones - e.g., additivity of both interventions in log-belief space, which results in distinct phases such that sudden and dramatic behavioral shifts can be induced by slightly changing intervention controls. Taken together, this work offers a unified account of prompt-based and activation-based control of LLM behavior, and a methodology for empirically predicting the effects of these interventions.

papers.title: Steering When Necessary: Flexible Steering Large Language Models with Backtracking
papers.research_question: How to dynamically determine the necessity and strength of intervention when steering large language models, and how to correct deviated tokens through backtracking?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a flexible activation steering framework with backtracking that dynamically determines intervention necessity and strength by tracking LLM internal states, and a backtracking mechanism to correct deviated tokens.
papers.conclusion: The FASB framework effectively steers LLMs by dynamically determining intervention necessity and strength, with backtracking correcting deviated tokens, and demonstrates strong performance across multiple tasks and models.
papers.key_findings:
FASB outperforms existing activation steering baselines on TruthfulQA and multiple-choice datasets.
Ablation studies show that adaptive intervention strength and the backtracking mechanism are crucial for performance.
The method generalizes to various LLMs of different sizes and architectures, and to out-of-distribution truthful benchmarks.
Performance improves with more attention heads and higher intervention strength, but informativeness may degrade with excessive intervention.
The method is effective even with limited training data for the probe.
papers.limitation:
The method may be used for malicious purposes (e.g., jailbreaking, toxic content generation).
The approach is hyperparameter-dependent and focused on QA tasks for specific behaviors (truthfulness, informativeness) on English datasets.
Evaluation uses LLM-based judges which may introduce errors.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many generation tasks. Nevertheless, effectively aligning them with desired behaviors remains a significant challenge. Activation steering is an effective and cost-efficient approach that directly modifies the activations of LLMs during the inference stage, aligning their responses with the desired behaviors and avoiding the high cost of fine-tuning. Existing methods typically indiscriminately intervene to all generations or rely solely on the question to determine intervention, which limits the accurate assessment of the intervention strength. To this end, we propose the Flexible Activation Steering with Backtracking (FASB) framework, which dynamically determines both the necessity and strength of intervention by tracking the internal states of the LLMs during generation, considering both the question and the generated content. Since intervening after detecting a deviation from the desired behavior is often too late, we further propose the backtracking mechanism to correct the deviated tokens and steer the LLMs toward the desired behavior. Extensive experiments on the TruthfulQA dataset and six multiple-choice datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms baselines. Our code will be released at https://github.com/gjw185/FASB.

papers.title: Fine-Grained Activation Steering: Steering Less, Achieving More
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be made more efficient and effective by moving from block-level to fine-grained atomic unit (AU) level interventions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes AUSteer, a fine-grained AU-level activation steering method that localizes discriminative atomic units via activation momentum and assigns adaptive steering strengths, achieving superior performance with far fewer interventions than block-level methods.
papers.conclusion: Fine-grained AU-level activation steering with AUSteer demonstrates that steering fewer activations can achieve more, significantly outperforming existing methods across diverse tasks and models.
papers.key_findings:
Block-level activations are heterogeneous, mixing beneficial, irrelevant, and harmful features, making block-level steering coarse and inefficient.
Steering at the AU level is more precise and effective; steering a small subset of beneficial AUs can outperform steering entire blocks.
AUSteer consistently outperforms state-of-the-art activation steering methods across diverse tasks while intervening on at most 100 activations.
Activation momentum is an effective metric for globally identifying discriminative AUs without layer-wise magnitude bias.
Adaptive steering that scales with input activation and AU discriminative power improves performance and reduces unnecessary perturbation.
papers.limitation: Reliance on contrastive sample pairs for computing activation momentum and steering vectors, which is an inherent limitation of existing activation-steering methods.
future_direction: Explore approaches to reduce or eliminate the requirement for contrastive pairs.
Investigate more principled methods to reduce task-dependent hyperparameter sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Activation steering has emerged as a cost-effective paradigm for modifying large language model (LLM) behaviors. Existing methods typically intervene at the block level, steering the bundled activations of selected attention heads, feedforward networks, or residual streams. However, we reveal that block-level activations are inherently heterogeneous, entangling beneficial, irrelevant, and harmful features, thereby rendering block-level steering coarse, inefficient, and intrusive. To investigate the root cause, we decompose block activations into fine-grained atomic unit (AU)-level activations, where each AU-level activation corresponds to a single dimension of the block activation, and each AU denotes a slice of the block weight matrix. Steering an AU-level activation is thus equivalent to steering its associated AU. Our theoretical and empirical analysis show that heterogeneity arises because different AUs or dimensions control distinct token distributions in LLM outputs. Hence, block-level steering inevitably moves helpful and harmful token directions together, which reduces efficiency. Restricting intervention to beneficial AUs yields more precise and effective steering. Building on this insight, we propose AUSteer, a simple and efficient method that operates at a finer granularity of the AU level. AUSteer first identifies discriminative AUs globally by computing activation momenta on contrastive samples. It then assigns adaptive steering strengths tailored to diverse inputs and selected AU activations. Comprehensive experiments on multiple LLMs and tasks show that AUSteer consistently surpasses advanced baselines while steering considerably fewer activations, demonstrating that steering less achieves more.

papers.title: Activation Steering with a Feedback Controller
papers.research_question: How can we develop a control-theoretic foundation for activation steering in large language models to achieve more robust and reliable behavioral control?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes PID Steering, a control-theoretic framework for activation steering in LLMs that uses a Proportional-Integral-Derivative controller to compute steering vectors, reducing steady-state error and improving stability compared to existing methods.
papers.conclusion: PID Steering provides a principled control-theoretic framework for activation steering, offering improved performance, stability, and interpretability for controlling LLM behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Existing activation steering methods (ActAdd, DirAblate, Mean-AcT) correspond to proportional (P) controllers and suffer from steady-state error.
PID Steering reduces steady-state error and overshoot by incorporating integral and derivative terms.
PID Steering outperforms existing methods in toxicity mitigation and jailbreaking tasks across multiple model families and scales.
The method is lightweight, modular, and integrates with existing steering paradigms.
Theoretical analysis shows PID Steering ensures input-to-state stability and reduces the first-overshoot amplitude.
papers.abstract: Controlling the behaviors of large language models (LLM) is fundamental to their safety alignment and reliable deployment. However, existing steering methods are primarily driven by empirical insights and lack theoretical performance guarantees. In this work, we develop a control-theoretic foundation for activation steering by showing that popular steering methods correspond to the proportional (P) controllers, with the steering vector serving as the feedback signal. Building on this finding, we propose Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) Steering, a principled framework that leverages the full PID controller for activation steering in LLMs. The proportional (P) term aligns activations with target semantic directions, the integral (I) term accumulates errors to enforce persistent corrections across layers, and the derivative (D) term mitigates overshoot by counteracting rapid activation changes. This closed-loop design yields interpretable error dynamics and connects activation steering to classical stability guarantees in control theory. Moreover, PID Steering is lightweight, modular, and readily integrates with state-of-the-art steering methods. Extensive experiments across multiple LLM families and benchmarks demonstrate that PID Steering consistently outperforms existing approaches, achieving more robust and reliable behavioral control.

papers.title: Painless Activation Steering: An Automated, Lightweight Approach for Post-Training Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do there exist activation steering (AS) methods that are both human-independent and adaptive to arbitrary models and arbitrary tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Painless Activation Steering (PAS), a family of fully automated, human-independent methods for activation steering that works with any labeled dataset, removing the need for manual prompt construction or feature annotation.
papers.conclusion: PAS provides a fast, lightweight, and practical automated option for post-training large language models, complementing weight- and prompt-based methods.
papers.key_findings:
PAS reliably improves performance on behavior tasks (bias, morality, alignment) but provides little benefit on intelligence-oriented tasks.
Introspective PAS variants (iPAS) perform best by constructing steering vectors from a model's own errors.
PAS complements existing methods, providing additional gains on top of In-Context Learning (ICL) and outperforming Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on TruthfulQA.
PAS generally does not cause catastrophic forgetting on control tasks, except at very high steering strengths.
PAS is effective even in small data regimes and is computationally and storage efficient compared to weight-based methods.
papers.limitation:
PAS is ineffective on intelligence-oriented tasks that require specialized knowledge or advanced reasoning capacity.
At very high steering strengths, PAS can cause catastrophic forgetting on tasks like Sycophancy and TruthfulQA.
PAS is mathematically equivalent to modifying a single bias vector, which may limit its expressivity compared to methods that update all weights.
future_direction: Extending PAS through multi-task multi-layer composition.
Exploring alternative extraction methods for steering vectors.
Investigating new use cases for the PAS framework.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) are typically post-trained for desired capabilities and behaviors via weight-based or prompt-based steering, but the former is time-consuming and expensive, and the latter is not precisely controllable and often requires manual trial-and-error. While activation steering (AS) promises a cheap, fast, and controllable alternative to the two existing post-training methods, current AS techniques require hand-crafted prompt pairs or labor-intensive feature annotation, making them more inconvenient than the plug-and-play methods such as Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). We introduce Painless Activation Steering (PAS), a family of fully automated methods that make AS readily usable with any given labeled dataset, with no need for prompt construction, feature labeling, or human intervention. We evaluate PAS on three open-weight models (Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-8B, and Nous-Hermes-2) and 18 tasks; we find that PAS reliably improves performance for behavior tasks, but not for intelligence-oriented tasks. The introspective variant (iPAS) delivers the strongest causal steering effects (10.1% on Bias, 5.2% on Morality, and 34.8% on Alignment). We also show PAS delivers additional gains on top of In-Context Learning (ICL) and SFT. PAS constructs a fast, lightweight activation vector that can be cheaply trained, easily stored, and activated at will. Our results provide a characterization of where AS helps, where it fails, and how to deploy it as a practical, automated LM post-training option.

papers.title: Scaling laws for activation steering with Llama 2 models and refusal mechanisms
papers.research_question: How does the effectiveness of the Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steering technique scale with model size, specifically for controlling refusal behavior in Llama 2 models?
papers.core_contribution: The effectiveness of Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) for steering model behavior diminishes with increasing model size, negative steering is more effective than positive steering, and steering is most effective when applied at early-mid layers.
papers.conclusion: Model alignment is complex and requires nuanced approaches to steer models effectively as they become larger, with future research needed to understand the interplay between alignment strategies, model architecture, and dataset characteristics.
papers.key_findings:
CAA is most effective when applied at early-mid layers (approximately 0.4 × total layer count).
The effectiveness of CAA diminishes with model size, making larger models harder to steer with the same vectors.
Negative steering (towards non-refusal) has more pronounced effects than positive steering across all model sizes.
The layer of peak steering effectiveness for positive and negative steering converges as model size increases.
The diminishing effectiveness might be because larger models 'drown out' the steering vector due to more downstream computation.
papers.limitation: The experiments were limited to the specific topic of refusal and the results may be different for different topics or prompting approaches.
future_direction: Feature steering with sparse autoencoders (SAE).
Modifying activation steering for larger models, e.g., scaling up steering vectors or injecting at multiple layers.
Experimenting with diverse model architectures (e.g., Mistral, BERT, BLOOM) to understand alignment differences.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) evolve in complexity and capability, the efficacy of less widely deployed alignment techniques are uncertain. Building on previous work on activation steering and contrastive activation addition (CAA), this paper explores the effectiveness of CAA with model scale using the family of Llama 2 models (7B, 13B, and 70B). CAA works by finding desirable 'directions' in the model's residual stream vector space using contrastive pairs (for example, hate to love) and adding this direction to the residual stream during the forward pass. It directly manipulates the residual stream and aims to extract features from language models to better control their outputs. Using answer matching questions centered around the refusal behavior, we found that 1) CAA is most effective when applied at early-mid layers. 2) The effectiveness of CAA diminishes with model size. 3) Negative steering has more pronounced effects than positive steering across all model sizes.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Thinking Language Models via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: Can reasoning behaviors in thinking language models be controlled using steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that reasoning behaviors in thinking LLMs are mediated by linear directions in the activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors extracted via difference of means and attribution patching.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a practical method for controlling reasoning behaviors in thinking models, opening new possibilities for fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Thinking models exhibit distinct reasoning behaviors such as backtracking, uncertainty estimation, and example testing.
These behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space.
Steering vectors extracted via difference of means can control these behaviors, increasing or decreasing their occurrence.
The steering approach works across different model architectures within the DeepSeek-R1-Distill family.
The method provides a practical tool for modulating reasoning capabilities in thinking models.
papers.limitation:
The automated annotation process using GPT-4o has occasionally produced false positives and false negatives in identifying reasoning patterns.
The generalization of these findings to other models that have undergone reward-based RL training instead of being fine-tuned on thinking models remains an open question.
future_direction: Developing more robust annotation methods, potentially incorporating multiple models or human validation.
Extending the research to a broader range of models to understand the universality of thinking mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to the development of thinking language models that generate extensive internal reasoning chains before producing responses. While these models achieve improved performance, controlling their reasoning processes remains challenging. This work presents a steering approach for thinking LLMs by analyzing and manipulating specific reasoning behaviors in DeepSeek-R1-Distill models. Through a systematic experiment on 500 tasks across 10 diverse categories, we identify several reasoning behaviors exhibited by thinking models, including expressing uncertainty, generating examples for hypothesis validation, and backtracking in reasoning chains. We demonstrate that these behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors. By extracting and applying these vectors, we provide a method to modulate specific aspects of the model's reasoning process, such as its tendency to backtrack or express uncertainty. Our approach offers practical tools for steering reasoning processes in thinking models in a controlled and interpretable manner. We validate our steering method using three DeepSeek-R1-Distill models, demonstrating consistent control across different model architectures.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether masked diffusion language models admit a single activation direction for inference-time control of safety-related behaviors, and how the diffusion architecture affects the accessibility and transferability of such representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces activation steering for masked diffusion language models, showing that refusal behavior is governed by a consistent low-dimensional activation subspace, and that steering can effectively control safety refusal with diffusion-specific properties such as accessibility from pre-instruction tokens.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that activation steering is an effective inference-time control method for MDLMs, with diffusion-specific accessibility and localization properties, and that safety representations are architecture-dependent.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal behavior in MDLMs is governed by a single low-dimensional activation direction, enabling large and consistent shifts in refusal behavior when applied globally during reverse diffusion.
Effective refusal directions in MDLMs can be extracted from pre-instruction tokens, unlike autoregressive models, due to non-causal parallel processing.
Activation steering is most effective during early denoising steps and in mid-to-late transformer layers, with the first diffusion block contributing disproportionately.
Refusal directions transfer robustly between English and Chinese within the same MDLM, but do not reliably transfer to an autoregressive model, indicating architecture-dependent safety representations.
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text through an iterative denoising process. They have recently gained attention due to mask-parallel decoding and competitive performance with autoregressive large language models. However, effective mechanisms for inference-time control and steering in MDLMs remain largely unexplored. We present an activation-steering framework for MDLMs that computes layer-wise steering vectors from a single forward pass using contrastive examples, without simulating the denoising trajectory. These directions are applied at every reverse-diffusion step, yielding an efficient inference-time control mechanism. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct demonstrate reliable modulation of high-level attributes, with ablations examining the effects of steering across transformer sub-modules and token scope (prompt vs.\ response).

papers.title: Exploring Diverse Generation Paths via Inference-time Stiefel Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can we increase the diversity of generation paths in language models at inference time without retraining, to avoid mode collapse and improve exploration in reasoning and creative tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces STARS, a training-free, inference-time activation steering method that maximizes the geometric volume of steered activations on the Stiefel manifold to diversify generation paths in language models.
papers.conclusion: STARS effectively diversifies generation paths in language models at inference time, improving performance on tasks that benefit from diverse outputs, such as test case generation and scientific idea generation.
papers.key_findings:
STARS consistently outperforms standard sampling methods in diversity metrics without sacrificing qualitative performance on test case generation and scientific idea benchmarks.
The method achieves higher line and branch coverage in test case generation and better originality in idea generation compared to temperature sampling.
A lightweight one-step update with a closed-form stepsize makes the method practical for real-time inference.
STARS promotes divergent activation vectors and, implicitly, divergent generation trajectories by enforcing orthogonality of steering interventions.
The method is robust across different temperature settings and model sizes.
papers.limitation:
A too large steering magnitude α may break the meaningful information in the hidden activations, leading to generation collapse.
In the dice rolling experiment, STARS does not achieve a fully uniform distribution across all outcomes, indicating room for improvement in achieving perfect diversity.
papers.abstract: Language models often default to a narrow set of high-probability outputs, leaving their generation paths homogeneous and prone to mode collapse. Sampling-based strategies inject randomness but still struggle to guarantee diversity across multiple concurrent generation runs. We address this limitation by introducing STARS ($\textbf{St}$iefel-based $\textbf{A}$ctivation Steering for Diverse $\textbf{R}$ea$\textbf{S}$oning), a training-free, inference-time intervention method that transforms activation steering into an exploration engine. At each token, STARS collects the hidden activations of concurrent generation runs and optimizes multiple additive steering directions jointly on the Stiefel manifold. STARS maximizes the geometric volume of the steered activations, while the Stiefel manifold induces orthogonality of the steering interventions. This formulation explicitly promotes divergent activation vectors of concurrent generation runs, and implicitly promotes divergent generation trajectories. This manifold optimization formulation can be solved using a Riemannian gradient descent algorithm with convergence guarantees, but this algorithm is too time-consuming for real-time inference. To guarantee low latency, we further design a lightweight one-step update with an aggressive, closed-form stepsize. For test case generation and scientific discovery benchmarks, STARS consistently outperforms standard sampling methods, achieving greater diversity without sacrificing qualitative performance.

papers.title: Analysing the Generalisation and Reliability ofSteering Vectors
papers.research_question: What are the reliability and generalisation properties of steering vectors for adjusting language model behaviour at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: This work rigorously investigates the reliability and generalization of steering vectors, showing they have substantial limitations both in- and out-of-distribution, including high variance in steerability across inputs and brittleness to prompt changes.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors in their current form are not a panacea for aligning model behavior at inference time; more work is required to ensure they reliably produce desired behavior in a generalisable way.
papers.key_findings:
In-distribution steerability is highly variable across inputs, with many examples being anti-steerable (steered in the opposite direction).
Steerability is affected by spurious factors like token and position bias, which are not fixable by simple dataset debiasing.
Out-of-distribution, steering vectors often generalize reasonably well but are brittle to reasonable changes in the prompt.
Steerability is mostly a property of the dataset used for extraction rather than the model architecture.
Similarity in the unsteered model behavior between source and target prompt settings is correlated with steering vector generalization.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a large number of datasets, but even more variety in the type of behavior being steered towards could be studied to ensure robustness.
The failures of steering vectors are not entirely understood, and it is unclear what potential mitigations could be applied.
Only two models are analyzed in this work, although they use different sizes, architectures, training data and algorithms.
future_direction: Investigating what causes steerability biases and whether other techniques for extracting and applying SVs can mitigate these biases.
Investigating methods to improve SV generalisation, and investigating scenarios where they generalise better or worse.
Developing methods to disentangle separate sub-behaviours in an unsupervised way for unsteerable behaviours.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) are a new approach to efficiently adjust language model behaviour at inference time by intervening on intermediate model activations. They have shown promise in terms of improving both capabilities and model alignment. However, the reliability and generalisation properties of this approach are unknown. In this work, we rigorously investigate these properties, and show that steering vectors have substantial limitations both in- and out-of-distribution. In-distribution, steerability is highly variable across different inputs. Depending on the concept, spurious biases can substantially contribute to how effective steering is for each input, presenting a challenge for the widespread use of steering vectors. Out-of-distribution, while steering vectors often generalise well, for several concepts they are brittle to reasonable changes in the prompt, resulting in them failing to generalise well. Overall, our findings show that while steering can work well in the right circumstances, there remain many technical difficulties of applying steering vectors to guide models' behaviour at scale.

papers.title: Steering Risk Preferences in Large Language Models by Aligning Behavioral and Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How can steering vectors be systematically identified to change LLM behavior? The paper proposes a principled approach by aligning latent representations from behavioral methods (Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with neural counterparts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for deriving steering vectors by aligning behavioral representations (elicited via MCMC with LLMs) with neural activations, enabling precise control of LLM risk preferences without retraining.
papers.conclusion: Self-alignment methods that align behavioral and neural representations offer an effective and principled means of controlling LLM behavior in risk-sensitive contexts.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors derived from aligned behavioral and neural representations (MCMC and Certainty Equivalent methods) outperform Contrastive Activation in steering risky decisions, risk perception, and text generation.
The optimal layer for steering varies: risk perception is more steerable in earlier layers, while risky decisions are more steerable in later layers.
The method allows precise control over risk preferences (risk-seeking vs. risk-averse) across different tasks.
Steering vectors transfer to tasks far from the original elicitation context.
The behavioral representation from MCMC reveals more nuanced risk preferences compared to the Certainty Equivalent method.
papers.limitation:
Further theoretical and mechanistic interpretability research is needed to establish a more concrete link between behaviorally elicited representations and their corresponding neural activations.
Modifying a Transformer’s residual stream is not uniformly effective across all layers; the success of such interventions is highly dependent on the layer selected. Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question.
This form of steering is limited in scope for proprietary models where weights are not accessible, restricting its broader applicability.
future_direction: Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question for future research.
Future research should consider developing new descriptive frameworks tailored to characterizing and predicting the risky choices of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Changing the behavior of large language models (LLMs) can be as straightforward as editing the Transformer's residual streams using appropriately constructed "steering vectors." These modifications to internal neural activations, a form of representation engineering, offer an effective and targeted means of influencing model behavior without retraining or fine-tuning the model. But how can such steering vectors be systematically identified? We propose a principled approach for uncovering steering vectors by aligning latent representations elicited through behavioral methods (specifically, Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with their neural counterparts. To evaluate this approach, we focus on extracting latent risk preferences from LLMs and steering their risk-related outputs using the aligned representations as steering vectors. We show that the resulting steering vectors successfully and reliably modulate LLM outputs in line with the targeted behavior.

papers.title: Interpretable LLM Guardrails via Sparse Representation Steering
papers.research_question: How can we achieve fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior to mitigate harmful, misleading, or biased content using sparse representation steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SRS, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to disentangle activations into monosemantic features and steer LLM behavior via sparse steering vectors, achieving fine-grained control while preserving output quality.
papers.conclusion: SRS enables precise and interpretable steering of LLM behavior using sparse representations, providing a reliable guardrail for safety, fairness, and truthfulness with superior performance over existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
SRS outperforms existing steering methods like CAA and SAE-TS in single-attribute and multi-attribute control tasks.
SRS maintains high linguistic quality, including grammatical correctness and language diversity, with minimal side effects.
SRS demonstrates robustness against diverse jailbreak prompts, achieving high defense rates.
Multi-attribute control with PCA composition strategy yields the best trade-off between control effectiveness and content quality.
Sparse features enable interpretable identification of attribute-relevant dimensions through KL divergence analysis.
papers.limitation: Multi-attribute steering strategies such as PCA may not fully capture complex relationships and conflicts between attributes.
future_direction: Layer-wise or component-wise multi-attribute steering to align interventions with semantic levels.
Context-aware and personalized steering based on semantic subdomains of prompts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities in generation tasks but are prone to producing harmful, misleading, or biased content, posing significant ethical and safety concerns. To mitigate such risks, representation engineering, which steer model behavior toward desired attributes by injecting carefully designed steering vectors into LLM's representations at inference time, has emerged as a promising alternative to fine-tuning approaches. However, due to the semantically entangled nature of LLM's representation, existing representation engineering methods still suffer from several limitations: limited fine-grained controllability, content quality degradation, and conflict in multi-attribute control. To overcome these challenges, we propose Sparse Representation Steering (SRS), a novel framework that achieves fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior by first disentangling internal activations into a sparse, semantically meaningful representation space, and then selectively steering relevant dimensions. Specifically, SRS leverages a pretrained Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) to transform dense, entangled activation patterns into a sparse monosemantic feature space. To identify relevant features, SRS contrasts sparse activations from positive and negative prompt pairs and measures their bidirectional KL divergence to locate dimensions most associated with the target attribute. We conduct comprehensive experiments on Gemma-2 series model across three alignment dimensions, i.e., safety, fairness, and truthfulness, to evaluate the effectiveness of SRS. Results show that SRS consistently outperforms existing steering methods, which achieves significantly improved controllability across both single and multiple attribute settings, while preserving high linguistic quality and general ability.

papers.title: Steer2Edit: From Activation Steering to Component-Level Editing
papers.research_question: Can steering vectors be reinterpreted as diagnostic signals to reveal how a target behavior is distributed across model components, and can this information be used to selectively modify those components via weight editing to achieve better attribute-utility trade-offs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces STEER2EDIT, a training-free framework that converts activation steering vectors into component-level rank-1 weight edits, achieving more favorable attribute-utility trade-offs by selectively redistributing behavioral influence across individual attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.conclusion: STEER2EDIT provides a principled, training-free framework for converting steering vectors into component-level weight edits, enabling precise behavioral control with favorable attribute-utility trade-offs and interpretable, architecture-preserving model modifications.
papers.key_findings:
STEER2EDIT consistently achieves superior attribute-utility trade-offs compared to activation steering: at matched downstream performance, it improves safety by up to 17.2%, increases truthfulness by 9.8%, and reduces reasoning length by 12.2% on average.
The method produces interpretable, sparse edits: safety and truthfulness control are mediated by a small subset of attention heads, while reasoning efficiency is governed by distributed MLP neuron edits.
The edits are closed-form, require no fine-tuning, and yield a standalone edited model that preserves the original architecture and standard forward pass.
Component importance scores (cosine similarity between steering vector and component output) and Elastic-Net regularization are critical for stable and sparse editing.
The framework provides a principled bridge between representation steering and weight editing, translating steering signals into interpretable parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Steering methods influence Large Language Model behavior by identifying semantic directions in hidden representations, but are typically realized through inference-time activation interventions that apply a fixed, global modification to the model's internal states. While effective, such interventions often induce unfavorable attribute-utility trade-offs under strong control, as they ignore the fact that many behaviors are governed by a small and heterogeneous subset of model components. We propose Steer2Edit, a theoretically grounded, training-free framework that transforms steering vectors from inference-time control signals into diagnostic signals for component-level rank-1 weight editing. Instead of uniformly injecting a steering direction during generation, Steer2Edit selectively redistributes behavioral influence across individual attention heads and MLP neurons, yielding interpretable edits that preserve the standard forward pass and remain compatible with optimized parallel inference. Across safety alignment, hallucination mitigation, and reasoning efficiency, Steer2Edit consistently achieves more favorable attribute-utility trade-offs: at matched downstream performance, it improves safety by up to 17.2%, increases truthfulness by 9.8%, and reduces reasoning length by 12.2% on average. Overall, Steer2Edit provides a principled bridge between representation steering and weight editing by translating steering signals into interpretable, training-free parameter updates.

papers.title: Analyzing the Generalization and Reliability of Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: What are the reliability and generalization properties of steering vectors in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that steering vectors have substantial limitations in reliability and generalization, with high variance in-distribution and imperfect generalization out-of-distribution.
papers.conclusion: Overall, steering vectors are not a panacea for aligning model behavior; more work is needed to ensure reliability and generalizability.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors exhibit high variance in steerability across inputs, with some inputs being anti-steerable.
Steerability is affected by spurious factors like token and position biases, leading to steerability bias.
Some behaviors are unsteerable, indicating limitations in linear representation.
Out-of-distribution, steerability generalizes reasonably but not perfectly, and is correlated with in-distribution performance.
Steerability is mostly a property of the dataset rather than the model, and generalization is predicted by model behavior similarity.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a large number of datasets but could benefit from even more variety in behaviors.
The failures of steering vectors are not entirely understood, and mitigations are unclear.
Only two models are analyzed, limiting the robustness of results.
future_direction: Investigating what causes steerability biases and how to mitigate them.
Improving SV generalization, especially when guiding models towards behaviors they do not normally produce.
Developing methods to disentangle separate sub-behaviors in an unsupervised way.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) have been proposed as an effective approach to adjust language model behaviour at inference time by intervening on intermediate model activations. They have shown promise in terms of improving both capabilities and model alignment. However, the reliability and generalisation properties of this approach are unknown. In this work, we rigorously investigate these properties, and show that steering vectors have substantial limitations both in- and out-of-distribution. In-distribution, steerability is highly variable across different inputs. Depending on the concept, spurious biases can substantially contribute to how effective steering is for each input, presenting a challenge for the widespread use of steering vectors. Out-of-distribution, while steering vectors often generalise well, for several concepts they are brittle to reasonable changes in the prompt, resulting in them failing to generalise well. Overall, our findings show that while steering can work well in the right circumstances, there remain technical difficulties of applying steering vectors to guide models' behaviour at scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/dtch1997/steering-bench

papers.title: Linearly Controlled Language Generation with Performative Guarantees
papers.research_question: How can we achieve controlled language generation with formal guarantees on output attributes, such as toxicity and sentiment, while maintaining text quality and computational efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Linear Semantic Control (LiSeCo), a gradient-free intervention method that uses control theory to dynamically steer activations in the latent space, guaranteeing that generated text meets pre-defined attribute constraints (e.g., toxicity, sentiment) while maintaining text quality.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LiSeCo offers a principled approach to controlled language generation with performative guarantees, effectively steering attributes like toxicity and sentiment while maintaining text quality.
papers.key_findings:
LiSeCo successfully reduces toxicity and negativity scores in generated text while preserving naturalness as measured by perplexity.
LiSeCo provides formal guarantees that activations lie within desired regions, leading to reliable steering of output attributes.
The method is computationally efficient, requiring only closed-form computations at inference time, with minimal impact on latency.
LiSeCo outperforms baselines like Activation Addition and AcT in fine-grained control over attribute scores.
The intervention is context-dependent and can be applied dynamically during generation without retraining the model.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical guarantees rely on the assumption that the attribute of interest is linearly separable in the latent space at each layer, which may not hold for all attributes.
The method requires training linear probes per layer, which adds an offline cost.
Evaluation is limited to English text; multilingual settings are not explored.
future_direction: Extending LiSeCo to multilingual settings.
Exploring non-linear control strategies.
Applying the method to other attributes and modalities.
papers.abstract: The increasing prevalence of Large Language Models (LMs) in critical applications highlights the need for controlled language generation strategies that are not only computationally efficient but that also enjoy performance guarantees. To achieve this, we use a common model of concept semantics as linearly represented in an LM's latent space. In particular, we take the view that natural language generation traces a trajectory in this continuous semantic space, realized by the language model's hidden activations. This view permits a control-theoretic treatment of text generation in latent space, in which we propose a lightweight, gradient-free intervention that dynamically steers trajectories away from regions corresponding to undesired meanings. In particular, we propose to directly intervene the activations of the token that is being generated in embedding space in an online fashion. Crucially, we do not simply steer activations towards a desirable region. Instead, our method relies on classical techniques from control theory to precisely control activations in a context-dependent way, and guarantees that they are brought into a specific pre-defined region of embedding space that corresponds to allowed semantics. Our intervention is computed in closed-form according to an optimal controller formulation, minimally impacting generation time. This control of the activations in embedding space allows for fine-grained steering of attributes of the generated sequence. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on different objectives -- toxicity avoidance and sentiment control -- while maintaining text quality.

papers.title: Steering Language Models in Multi-Token Generation: A Case Study on Tense and Aspect
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode the grammatical features of tense and aspect internally, and how can we causally control these features during multi-token generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies orthogonal directions for tense and aspect in LLM residual space using LDA and demonstrates causal control via steering, showing that effective steering depends on strength, location, and duration to minimize side effects like topic shift and degeneration.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLMs encode tense and aspect in orthogonal, human-like grammatical structures, and steering can verify causality but requires careful tuning of parameters to avoid side effects, indicating it is not yet a perfect control method.
papers.key_findings:
Tense and aspect are encoded as distinct, orthogonal directions in residual space, forming structured subspaces.
Steering these directions can causally control the grammatical features in multi-token generation across different tasks.
Steering effectiveness varies by task and target, with tense easier to steer than aspect, and is influenced by activation norms and model architecture.
Steering strength, location, and duration are crucial parameters; improper settings lead to side effects like topic shift and degeneration.
Subtracting the source concept vector (TA+SS) can reduce selectivity, but projection subtraction (TA+Proj-SS) mitigates this issue.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on English, which has a very regular inflection system, and tense and aspect are only two of six known strategies for expressing temporal information in language.
The analysis focuses on steering grammatical properties in three tasks, and side effects such as topic shift may manifest differently when steering other concepts like sentiment.
future_direction: Investigate mechanism-independent time representations (e.g., consistent representation of 'past' in different surface forms).
Explore language-independent tense representations (e.g., cross-lingual past-present contrast).
Expand the range of tasks and steering targets to identify more general conditions for effective steering.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are able to generate grammatically well-formed text, but how do they encode their syntactic knowledge internally? While prior work has focused largely on binary grammatical contrasts, in this work, we study the representation and control of two multidimensional hierarchical grammar phenomena - verb tense and aspect - and for each, identify distinct, orthogonal directions in residual space using linear discriminant analysis. Next, we demonstrate causal control over both grammatical features through concept steering across three generation tasks. Then, we use these identified features in a case study to investigate factors influencing effective steering in multi-token generation. We find that steering strength, location, and duration are crucial parameters for reducing undesirable side effects such as topic shift and degeneration. Our findings suggest that models encode tense and aspect in structurally organized, human-like ways, but effective control of such features during generation is sensitive to multiple factors and requires manual tuning or automated optimization.

papers.title: Why Steering Works: Toward a Unified View of Language Model Parameter Dynamics
papers.research_question: How can we unify different LLM control methods (local weight fine-tuning, LoRA, activation steering) under a single framework, and what are the dynamics of preference and utility in these methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a unified dynamic weight update framework for LLM control methods, introduces a preference-utility analysis revealing a consistent trade-off, and proposes a new steering method (SPLIT) that improves preference while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a unified dynamic weight update framework that reveals a consistent preference-utility decay pattern and introduces a joint optimization method (SPLIT) that improves preference while mitigating utility degradation across diverse intervention forms.
papers.key_findings:
Different intervention methods (local weight, LoRA, activation steering) can be unified as dynamic weight updates.
There is a consistent trade-off between preference and utility: stronger control increases preference but reduces utility.
The activation manifold perspective explains this: control shifts representations along target-concept directions, and utility declines when representations are pushed off the manifold.
The proposed SPLIT method improves preference while better preserving utility compared to baselines.
papers.limitation:
The analysis assumes model representations lie near a well-structured activation manifold, which may not hold for extremely large or highly diverse models.
Experiments focus primarily on attribute-level control, leaving applicability to complex multi-turn reasoning or safety-critical content largely unexplored.
The proposed training objective does not guarantee complete avoidance of undesirable side effects such as subtle instruction violations or context drift under extreme control strengths.
Generalization to adaptive or dynamically varying control signals requires further investigation.
papers.abstract: Methods for controlling large language models (LLMs), including local weight fine-tuning, LoRA-based adaptation, and activation-based interventions, are often studied in isolation, obscuring their connections and making comparison difficult. In this work, we present a unified view that frames these interventions as dynamic weight updates induced by a control signal, placing them within a single conceptual framework. Building on this view, we propose a unified preference-utility analysis that separates control effects into preference, defined as the tendency toward a target concept, and utility, defined as coherent and task-valid generation, and measures both on a shared log-odds scale using polarity-paired contrastive examples. Across methods, we observe a consistent trade-off between preference and utility: stronger control increases preference while predictably reducing utility. We further explain this behavior through an activation manifold perspective, in which control shifts representations along target-concept directions to enhance preference, while utility declines primarily when interventions push representations off the model's valid-generation manifold. Finally, we introduce a new steering approach SPLIT guided by this analysis that improves preference while better preserving utility. Code is available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit/blob/main/examples/SPLIT.md.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Bias Mitigation: An Interpretable Approach to Safer LLMs
papers.research_question: Can bias in large language models be detected and mitigated by probing internal activations and applying steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretability-based system that uses linear probes to detect bias in LLM activations and applies steering vectors to mitigate biased outputs in real-time.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that bias can be detected and mitigated through activation steering, offering a transparent method for improving LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on internal activations can detect bias with near-perfect accuracy in later layers of gpt2-large.
Bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers, as shown by increasing probe accuracy.
Steering vectors computed from activation differences can successfully alter biased completions toward more neutral alternatives during inference.
The method provides a direct and interpretable approach to bias mitigation without modifying model weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted only on gpt2-large, limiting generalizability to other models.
The training dataset is synthetic, which may not fully represent real-world bias.
future_direction: Investigate whether findings generalize to other model architectures and sizes (e.g., Llama, Mistral).
Validate techniques on real-world datasets of hate speech or bias (e.g., HateXplain, CivilComments).
Explore the use of non-linear probes or more sophisticated steering techniques for more precise control.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integrated into societal systems, the risk of them perpetuating and amplifying harmful biases becomes a critical safety concern. Traditional methods for mitigating bias often rely on data filtering or post-hoc output moderation, which treat the model as an opaque black box. In this work, we introduce a complete, end-to-end system that uses techniques from mechanistic interpretability to both identify and actively mitigate bias directly within a model's internal workings. Our method involves two primary stages. First, we train linear "probes" on the internal activations of a model to detect the latent representations of various biases (e.g., gender, race, age). Our experiments on \texttt{gpt2-large} demonstrate that these probes can identify biased content with near-perfect accuracy, revealing that bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers. Second, we leverage these findings to compute "steering vectors" by contrasting the model's activation patterns for biased and neutral statements. By adding these vectors during inference, we can actively steer the model's generative process away from producing harmful, stereotypical, or biased content in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of this activation steering technique, showing that it successfully alters biased completions toward more neutral alternatives. We present our work as a robust and reproducible system that offers a more direct and interpretable approach to building safer and more accountable LLMs.

papers.title: LinEAS: End-to-end Learning of Activation Steering with a Distributional Loss
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently control generative models by steering activations with a global distributional loss that requires low data and is modality-agnostic?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LinEAS, a method for activation steering that uses a global distributional loss to jointly learn affine transformations across layers, enabling effective control with low data and automatic neuron selection via sparsity regularization.
papers.conclusion: LinEAS is an effective method for activation steering, offering improved controllability and robustness by learning lightweight interventions with a global distributional loss.
papers.key_findings:
LinEAS outperforms existing activation steering methods on toxicity mitigation in LLMs and style control in text-to-image models.
LinEAS requires only a handful of unpaired samples (e.g., 32) to be effective.
The global loss and joint optimization across layers lead to more robust interventions and better preservation of model utility.
Sparsity regularization allows automatic selection of neurons and layers, reducing the intervention support by 100x.
LinEAS provides a continuous intervention strength parameter, allowing fine-grained control.
papers.limitation: The method requires access to intermediate activations, which may not be available in all settings.
future_direction: Extending LinEAS to other modalities and tasks.
Investigating the theoretical properties of the distributional loss.
papers.abstract: The growing use of generative models in daily life calls for efficient mechanisms to control their generation, to e.g., produce safe content or provide users with tools to explore style changes. Ideally, such mechanisms should require low volume of unpaired data (i.e., without explicit preference), and should be cheap, both at train and inference time, while preserving output quality. Recent research has shown that such mechanisms can be obtained by intervening exclusively on model activations, with the goal of correcting distributional differences between activations seen when using prompts from a source vs. a target set (e.g., toxic and non-toxic sentences). While cheap, these fast methods are inherently crude: their maps are tuned locally, not accounting for their impact on downstream layers, resulting in interventions that cause unintended shifts when used out-of-sample. We propose in this work linear end-to-end activation steering (LinEAS), an approach trained with a global loss that accounts simultaneously for all layer-wise distributional shifts. In addition to being more robust, the loss used to train LinEAS can be regularized with sparsifying norms, which can automatically carry out neuron selection. LinEAS only requires a handful of unpaired samples to be effective, and beats similar baselines on toxicity mitigation in language models, becoming competitive with oracle-dependent methods that have access to strong supervision. LinEAS is modality-agnostic and we empirically find that it outperforms existing activation steering methods at mitigating and including new concepts at the output of single-step text-to-image generation models.

papers.title: Angular Steering: Behavior Control via Rotation in Activation Space
papers.research_question: How can we control specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Angular Steering, a rotation-based framework for fine-grained behavior control in LLMs that generalizes existing activation steering methods and maintains general language modeling performance.
papers.conclusion: Angular Steering offers a principled, flexible, and robust framework for behavior control in LLMs, enabling fine-grained modulation while preserving general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors like refusal and compliance by rotating activations in a fixed 2D subspace.
The method generalizes existing activation addition and directional ablation techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework.
Angular Steering maintains general language modeling performance (e.g., on TINYBENCHMARKS) while effectively steering behavior.
Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant, improves robustness and coherence by rotating only activations aligned with the target feature.
Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show the method's flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches.
papers.limitation: The method requires a contrastive dataset to extract the feature direction, which may not always be available.
future_direction: Extending Angular Steering to multi-feature steering and dynamic plane selection.
papers.abstract: Controlling specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities is a central challenge for safe and reliable artificial intelligence deployment. Current steering methods, such as vector addition and directional ablation, are constrained within a two-dimensional subspace defined by the activation and feature direction, making them sensitive to chosen parameters and potentially affecting unrelated features due to unintended interactions in activation space. We introduce Angular Steering, a novel and flexible method for behavior modulation that operates by rotating activations within a fixed two-dimensional subspace. By formulating steering as a geometric rotation toward or away from a target behavior direction, Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors such as refusal and compliance. We demonstrate this method using refusal steering emotion steering as use cases. Additionally, we propose Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant that rotates only activations aligned with the target feature, further enhancing stability and coherence. Angular Steering generalizes existing addition and orthogonalization techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework, simplifying parameter selection and maintaining model stability across a broader range of adjustments. Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show that Angular Steering achieves robust behavioral control while maintaining general language modeling performance, underscoring its flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/lone17/angular-steering/.

papers.title: Mitigating Content Effects on Reasoning in Language Models through Fine-Grained Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can content biases in reasoning be mitigated through activation steering in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces K-CAST, a fine-grained conditional activation steering method that effectively reduces content biases in reasoning, improving formal reasoning accuracy by up to 15%.
papers.conclusion: Activation-level interventions offer a scalable inference-time strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive steering methods enable linear control over content biases in reasoning.
Static steering is insufficient to debias all tested models.
K-CAST reduces biases on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy.
Steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations and incurs minimal side effects on multilingual language modeling capabilities.
Steering vectors can partially generalize to different out-of-distribution reasoning tasks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are performed on LLMs of up to 9 billion parameters due to computational constraints.
The study focuses mainly on synthetically generated tasks, which may not fully capture real-world applications.
future_direction: Applying the steering methodology to larger models.
Assessing how steering for content effect can impact real-world applications in critical domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently demonstrate reasoning limitations, often conflating content plausibility (i.e., material inference) with logical validity (i.e., formal inference). This can result in biased inferences, where plausible arguments are incorrectly deemed logically valid or vice versa. Mitigating this limitation is critical, as it undermines the trustworthiness and generalizability of LLMs in applications that demand rigorous logical consistency. This paper investigates the problem of mitigating content biases on formal reasoning through activation steering. Specifically, we curate a controlled syllogistic reasoning dataset to disentangle formal validity from content plausibility. After localising the layers responsible for formal and material inference, we investigate contrastive activation steering methods for test-time interventions. An extensive empirical analysis on different LLMs reveals that contrastive steering consistently supports linear control over content biases. However, we observe that a static approach is insufficient for improving all the tested models. We then leverage the possibility to control content effects by dynamically determining the value of the steering parameters via fine-grained conditional methods. We found that conditional steering is effective on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy with a newly introduced kNN-based method (K-CAST). Finally, additional experiments reveal that steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations, incurs minimal side effects on language modeling capabilities, and can partially generalize to out-of-distribution reasoning tasks. Practically, this paper demonstrates that activation-level interventions can offer a scalable strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased formal reasoning.

papers.title: Steering Large Language Model Activations in Sparse Spaces
papers.research_question: How can we steer large language model behavior in a more interpretable and fine-grained way by leveraging sparse representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Steering (SAS), a method that uses sparse autoencoders to extract interpretable steering vectors from contrastive prompt pairs, enabling precise and modular control over LLM behavior during inference.
papers.conclusion: SAS provides an effective framework for steering LLM behavior in sparse spaces, offering improved interpretability and fine-grained control compared to dense activation steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAS vectors enable nuanced behavioral modulation and finer-grained control over LLM outputs.
Scaling sparse autoencoders (increasing dictionary size) improves the monosemanticity of the extracted SAS vectors.
Sparse representations allow for modular control, enabling fine-grained behaviors to be composed simultaneously.
papers.abstract: A key challenge in AI alignment is guiding large language models (LLMs) to follow desired behaviors at test time. Activation steering, which modifies internal model activations during inference, offers a potential solution. However, prior work in dense activation spaces struggles with superposition, wherein multiple features become entangled, limiting interpretability and precise control. In contrast, sparse representations provide an untapped opportunity for more interpretable behavior modulation. In this work, we introduce sparse activation steering (SAS), a method that leverages sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to steer LLM behavior in sparse spaces. By isolating behavior-specific features through a contrastive prompt-pairing approach, we define a set of features that can selectively reinforce or suppress behaviors. Experiments on Gemma 2 LLMs show that SAS vectors enable nuanced behavioral modulation and finer-grained control. Furthermore, scaling SAEs improves monosemanticity of SAS vectors, suggesting more reliable and interpretable interventions.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by modifying their activations during inference? The paper introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) to control model behaviors.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method to steer language models by adding computed steering vectors to the residual stream, which effectively controls targeted behaviors with minimal impact on general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behaviors and insights into linear representations of abstract concepts in models.
papers.key_findings:
CAA effectively steers Llama 2 Chat models on multiple alignment-relevant behaviors, with optimal layers around layer 13 for 7B and 14-15 for 13B.
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks and works alongside system prompting and finetuning.
CAA has minimal negative impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU and can slightly improve truthfulness on TruthfulQA when subtracting sycophancy.
Steering vectors exhibit intuitive similarity with token activations relevant to the behavior and transfer well across layers and between base and chat models.
The representations of behaviors are linearly separable in the residual stream, and CAA vectors capture these directions.
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluations may be sensitive to prompt wording and have biases, though manual checks show consistency.
Finetuning baselines were not fully optimized (e.g., learning rate, epochs, loss function), so CAA's relative effect might be smaller with better finetuning.
Prompting baselines may not be fully optimized, and better prompts might achieve stronger effects.
Vector normalization choices (not normalizing across layers) could affect layer optimality results.
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions instead of all tokens after the prompt.
Steering outside the residual stream, e.g., after MLP layers.
Application to red-teaming to trigger unwanted behaviors more efficiently.
papers.abstract: We introduce Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), an innovative method for steering language models by modifying their activations during forward passes. CAA computes "steering vectors" by averaging the difference in residual stream activations between pairs of positive and negative examples of a particular behavior, such as factual versus hallucinatory responses. During inference, these steering vectors are added at all token positions after the user's prompt with either a positive or negative coefficient, allowing precise control over the degree of the targeted behavior. We evaluate CAA's effectiveness on Llama 2 Chat using multiple-choice behavioral question datasets and open-ended generation tasks. We demonstrate that CAA significantly alters model behavior, is effective over and on top of traditional methods like finetuning and system prompt design, and minimally reduces capabilities. Moreover, we gain deeper insights into CAA's mechanisms by employing various activation space interpretation methods. CAA accurately steers model outputs and sheds light on how high-level concepts are represented in Large Language Models (LLMs).

papers.title: LF-Steering: Latent Feature Activation Steering for Enhancing Semantic Consistency in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we precisely identify and modify latent feature representations to improve the semantic consistency of Large Language Models (LLMs) when responding to semantically equivalent paraphrased inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LF-Steering, a novel activation steering method that uses a sparse autoencoder (SAE) to decompose transformer layer hidden states into a sparsely activated, higher-dimensional feature space, enabling precise identification and adjustment of features responsible for semantic inconsistency to improve LLM performance.
