SeqBoat achieves competitive performance on speech classification (Speech Commands) and language modeling (enwik8) with improved efficiency.
papers.limitation:
The current implementation of SMA is I/O bounded due to copying large tensors with scatter operations, and no custom fused kernels were used for memory bandwidth optimization.
Experiments were limited to models of moderate size due to computational resource constraints, leaving scalability to larger models uncertain.
future_direction: Explore the scaling behavior of SMA and how to incorporate it with pre-trained large language models.
Investigate the interpretability of module activation patterns and their correlation with input tokens or model predictions.
Scale up SMA with a large number of modules, potentially impacting Mixture-of-Experts research.
papers.abstract: Recent hybrid models combining Linear State Space Models (SSMs) with self-attention mechanisms have demonstrated impressive results across a range of sequence modeling tasks. However, current approaches apply attention modules statically and uniformly to all elements in the input sequences, leading to sub-optimal quality-efficiency trade-offs. To address this limitation, we introduce Sparse Modular Activation (SMA), a general mechanism enabling neural networks to sparsely and dynamically activate sub-modules for sequence elements in a differentiable manner. Through allowing each element to skip non-activated sub-modules, SMA reduces computation and memory consumption of neural networks at both training and inference stages. To validate the effectiveness of SMA on sequence modeling, we design a novel neural architecture, SeqBoat, which employs SMA to sparsely activate a Gated Attention Unit (GAU) based on the state representations learned from an SSM. By constraining the GAU to only conduct local attention on the activated inputs, SeqBoat can achieve linear inference complexity with theoretically infinite attention span, and provide substantially better quality-efficiency trade-off than the chunking-based models. With experiments on a wide range of tasks, including long sequence modeling, speech classification and language modeling, SeqBoat brings new state-of-the-art results among hybrid models with linear complexity, and reveals the amount of attention needed for each task through the learned sparse activation patterns. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/renll/SeqBoat.

papers.title: Genome-Factory: An Integrated Library for Tuning, Deploying, and Interpreting Genomic Models
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GENOME-FACTORY, a unified Python library that streamlines the workflow for genomic model development, including data collection, tuning, inference, benchmarking, and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: GENOME-FACTORY is a unified and modular Python framework that streamlines the tuning, deployment, and interpretation of genomic models, lowering the technical barrier to using large-scale models in genomics research.
papers.key_findings:
GENOME-FACTORY supports diverse genomic models and three fine-tuning methods (full, LoRA, adapter).
Adapter tuning is the most efficient in memory and throughput, while full fine-tuning and LoRA achieve higher performance.
The library enables biological interpretation of model embeddings via sparse auto-encoders, identifying latent units correlated with sequence length.
The framework is validated on downstream tasks using two benchmarks, showing practical utility.
The library provides user-friendly interfaces (CLI and WebUI) for accessibility.
papers.limitation:
Due to compute cost, full fine-tuning for EVO (7B) is not considered.
Traditional computational biology techniques (e.g., PWM scanning, HMM-based motif finding) are not incorporated.
Only three fine-tuning methods are included; future plans to include more advanced techniques.
future_direction: Tracking state-of-the-art genomic models and updating the repertoire.
Incorporating novel training strategies and broadening integrated genomic tasks and benchmarks.
Advancing the Biological Interpreter for richer genomic interpretability.
papers.abstract: We introduce Genome-Factory, an integrated Python library for tuning, deploying, and interpreting genomic models. Our core contribution is to simplify and unify the workflow for genomic model development: data collection, model tuning, inference, benchmarking, and interpretability. For data collection, Genome-Factory offers an automated pipeline to download genomic sequences and preprocess them. It also includes quality control, such as GC content normalization. For model tuning, Genome-Factory supports three approaches: full-parameter, low-rank adaptation, and adapter-based fine-tuning. It is compatible with a wide range of genomic models. For inference, Genome-Factory enables both embedding extraction and DNA sequence generation. For benchmarking, we include two existing benchmarks and provide a flexible interface for users to incorporate additional benchmarks. For interpretability, Genome-Factory introduces the first open-source biological interpreter based on a sparse auto-encoder. This module disentangles embeddings into sparse, near-monosemantic latent units and links them to interpretable genomic features by regressing on external readouts. To improve accessibility, Genome-Factory features both a zero-code command-line interface and a user-friendly web interface. We validate the utility of Genome-Factory across three dimensions: (i) Compatibility with diverse models and fine-tuning methods; (ii) Benchmarking downstream performance using two open-source benchmarks; (iii) Biological interpretation of learned representations with DNABERT-2. These results highlight its end-to-end usability and practical value for real-world genomic analysis.

papers.title: A Markov Categorical Framework for Language Modeling
papers.research_question: How can we provide a unified theoretical understanding of the internal mechanisms of autoregressive language models, connecting training objectives, representation geometry, and model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Markov categorical framework that unifies the analysis of training objective, representation geometry, and model capabilities, providing an information-theoretic rationale for speculative decoding and showing how NLL induces spectral alignment in representations.
papers.conclusion: The Markov categorical framework offers a unified mathematical language to connect information flow, representation geometry, and training objectives, providing a powerful new lens for understanding language models.
papers.key_findings:
The framework provides a formal, information-theoretic rationale for the success of speculative decoding methods by quantifying the information surplus in a model's hidden state about future tokens.
The standard negative log-likelihood (NLL) objective compels the model to learn the data's intrinsic conditional uncertainty, formalized using categorical entropy.
Under a linear-softmax head with bounded features, minimizing NLL induces spectral alignment: the learned representation space aligns with the eigenspectrum of a predictive similarity operator.
papers.abstract: Autoregressive language models achieve remarkable performance, yet a unified theory explaining their internal mechanisms, how training shapes their representations, and enables complex behaviors, remains elusive. We introduce a new analytical framework that models the single-step generation process as a composition of information-processing stages using the language of Markov categories. This compositional perspective provides a unified mathematical language to connect three critical aspects of language modeling that are typically studied in isolation: the training objective, the geometry of the learned representation space, and practical model capabilities. First, our framework provides a precise information-theoretic rationale for the success of multi-token prediction methods like speculative decoding, quantifying the information surplus a model's hidden state contains about tokens beyond the immediate next one. Second, we clarify how the standard negative log-likelihood (NLL) objective compels the model to learn not just the next word, but also the data's intrinsic conditional uncertainty, a process we formalize using categorical entropy. Our central result shows that, under a linear-softmax head with bounded features, minimizing NLL induces spectral alignment: the learned representation space aligns with the eigenspectrum of a predictive similarity operator. This work presents a powerful new lens for understanding how information flows through a model and how the training objective shapes its internal geometry.

papers.title: Analyze Feature Flow to Enhance Interpretation and Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do features discovered by sparse autoencoders evolve across consecutive layers of large language models, and how can this understanding be used for interpretability and model steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a data-free cosine similarity method to map Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features across transformer layers, creating flow graphs that reveal feature evolution and enable precise model steering through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed cross-layer feature mapping framework provides granular interpretability of feature evolution in LLMs and offers a new, transparent method for steering model behavior through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Cosine similarity between SAE decoder weights effectively identifies feature relationships across layers, validated against activation correlations.
Feature formation follows distinct patterns: early layers show high entropy and feature birth, middle layers stabilize, and later layers primarily propagate existing features.
Deactivating predecessor features identified by the top-1 cosine match is causally effective, outperforming random selection.
Multi-layer steering using flow graphs is more effective and less sensitive to hyperparameters than single-layer interventions.
Flow graphs provide mechanistic insights, revealing how semantic meaning (e.g., 'particle physics') evolves and transforms across the model's computational pathway.
papers.limitation: The current steering procedure operates locally on hidden states and may not fully redirect the model's computational trajectory to a different 'minima' for truly efficient deactivation or activation.
future_direction: Further research on flow graphs as a unit of study for model interpretability.
Extending the steering experiments and flow graph analysis to other model architectures like Llama Scope.
Investigating the method's applicability and performance across a wider range of models and SAE training configurations.
papers.abstract: We introduce a new approach to systematically map features discovered by sparse autoencoder across consecutive layers of large language models, extending earlier work that examined inter-layer feature links. By using a data-free cosine similarity technique, we trace how specific features persist, transform, or first appear at each stage. This method yields granular flow graphs of feature evolution, enabling fine-grained interpretability and mechanistic insights into model computations. Crucially, we demonstrate how these cross-layer feature maps facilitate direct steering of model behavior by amplifying or suppressing chosen features, achieving targeted thematic control in text generation. Together, our findings highlight the utility of a causal, cross-layer interpretability framework that not only clarifies how features develop through forward passes but also provides new means for transparent manipulation of large language models.

papers.title: Representation Engineering for Large-Language Models: Survey and Research Challenges
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the goals, methods, and challenges of representation engineering as an approach to make large-language models more predictable and controllable.
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes the goals and methods of representation engineering, providing a cohesive survey of this emerging discipline and outlining a research agenda for building more predictable and controllable large-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation engineering is a promising approach for enhancing LLM transparency and control, and it provides a clear agenda for future research to address current challenges.
papers.key_findings:
Representation engineering uses contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations, offering a top-down approach to model interpretability and control.
It compares favorably with alternative approaches like mechanistic interpretability and prompt-engineering in certain aspects.
Risks include performance degradation, increased compute time, and steerability issues.
The linear representation hypothesis underpins representation engineering, but its strong form may not hold, limiting generalizability.
Future research should focus on dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.limitation:
Performance decrease, compute time increases, and steerability issues.
The strong linear representation hypothesis may not hold, limiting generalized interventions.
future_direction: Build predictable, dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large-language models are capable of completing a variety of tasks, but remain unpredictable and intractable. Representation engineering seeks to resolve this problem through a new approach utilizing samples of contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations of concepts such as honesty, harmfulness or power-seeking. We formalize the goals and methods of representation engineering to present a cohesive picture of work in this emerging discipline. We compare it with alternative approaches, such as mechanistic interpretability, prompt-engineering and fine-tuning. We outline risks such as performance decrease, compute time increases and steerability issues. We present a clear agenda for future research to build predictable, dynamic, safe and personalizable LLMs.

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-Correction in LLMs: Towards Explainable Prompting via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does intrinsic self-correction prompting act as representation steering along interpretable latent directions?
papers.core_contribution: Intrinsic self-correction in LLMs functions by steering hidden representations along interpretable latent directions, as evidenced by alignment between prompt-induced shifts and steering vectors and causal verification via activation addition.
papers.conclusion: The findings link self-correction prompting to representation steering along interpretable latent directions, highlighting the role of interpretability methods in understanding prompt-driven LLM phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Prompt-induced shifts in self-correction align with steering vectors constructed from contrastive pairs.
Activation injection with steering vectors causally reproduces behavioral changes in toxicity.
Detoxification is effective even with weak prompts, while toxification requires strong prompts.
Most of the behavioral change occurs in the first self-correction round.
Alignment between shifts and vectors peaks in mid-to-late layers for some models.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to toxicity-related behaviors and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other prompt-driven phenomena such as chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: Intrinsic self-correction refers to the phenomenon where a language model refines its own outputs purely through prompting, without external feedback or parameter updates. While this approach improves performance across diverse tasks, its mechanism remains unclear. We show that intrinsic self-correction functions by steering hidden representations along interpretable latent directions, as evidenced by both alignment analysis and activation interventions. To achieve this, we analyze intrinsic self-correction via the representation shift induced by prompting. In parallel, we construct interpretable latent directions with contrastive pairs and verify the causal effect of these directions via activation addition. Evaluating six open-source LLMs, our results demonstrate that prompt-induced representation shifts in text detoxification and text toxification consistently align with latent directions constructed from contrastive pairs. In detoxification, the shifts align with the non-toxic direction; in toxification, they align with the toxic direction. These findings suggest that representation steering is the mechanistic driver of intrinsic self-correction. Our analysis highlights that understanding model internals offers a direct route to analyzing the mechanisms of prompt-driven LLM behaviors.

papers.title: Does Transformer Interpretability Transfer to RNNs?
papers.research_question: Does transformer interpretability transfer to RNNs? Specifically, do contrastive activation addition, the tuned lens, and methods for eliciting latent knowledge work on RNNs like Mamba and RWKV?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that popular transformer interpretability methods (contrastive activation addition, the tuned lens, and methods for eliciting latent knowledge) transfer to state-of-the-art RNN architectures, and that the compressed state of RNNs can be used to enhance activation addition for steering.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability tools designed for transformers largely work out-of-the-box for RNNs, with similar performance, and the compressed state of RNNs can be used to enhance activation addition for steering.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) is effective for steering RNNs, with middle layers showing the greatest effect.
State steering, using the internal state of RNNs, is possible and can be combined with activation steering, though the effects are not additive.
The tuned lens can be applied to RNNs, with perplexity decreasing monotonically with depth, similar to transformers.
Linear probes trained on 'Alice' contexts can predict the correct answer in 'Bob' contexts for RNNs, similar to transformers.
papers.limitation: The work did not explore mechanistic or circuit-based interpretability tools, focusing instead on representation-based methods.
future_direction: Further exploration of the RNN state for extracting latent knowledge or predictions.
Examination of the applicability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to RNNs.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in recurrent neural network architectures, such as Mamba and RWKV, have enabled RNNs to match or exceed the performance of equal-size transformers in terms of language modeling perplexity and downstream evaluations, suggesting that future systems may be built on completely new architectures. In this paper, we examine if selected interpretability methods originally designed for transformer language models will transfer to these up-and-coming recurrent architectures. Specifically, we focus on steering model outputs via contrastive activation addition, on eliciting latent predictions via the tuned lens, and eliciting latent knowledge from models fine-tuned to produce false outputs under certain conditions. Our results show that most of these techniques are effective when applied to RNNs, and we show that it is possible to improve some of them by taking advantage of RNNs' compressed state.

papers.title: The Confidence Manifold: Geometric Structure of Correctness Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the geometric structure of correctness representations in language models, and how can it be used for efficient detection of model errors?
papers.core_contribution: The discriminative signal for correctness in language models is low-dimensional (3-8 dimensions) and linearly separable; centroid distance in this subspace matches trained probe performance, enabling few-shot error detection.
papers.conclusion: The confidence manifold is simpler than expected, with a low-dimensional linear structure, enabling efficient geometric detection of model errors via centroid distance.
papers.key_findings:
The confidence signal occupies 3-8 dimensions, and adding more dimensions hurts performance.
The signal is linearly separable; no nonlinear classifier improves over linear probes.
Centroid distance in the low-dimensional subspace matches trained probe performance, enabling few-shot detection with minimal labels.
Internal probes achieve high AUC (0.80-0.97) while output-based methods like semantic entropy perform poorly (0.44-0.64).
Activation steering validates causality: the learned direction produces monotonic, 10.9 percentage point changes in error rates.
papers.limitation: The signal does not transfer well to tasks like HaluEval (summarization faithfulness), indicating specificity to factual QA.
papers.abstract: When a language model asserts that "the capital of Australia is Sydney," does it know this is wrong? We characterize the geometry of correctness representations across 9 models from 5 architecture families. The structure is simple: the discriminative signal occupies 3-8 dimensions, performance degrades with additional dimensions, and no nonlinear classifier improves over linear separation. Centroid distance in the low-dimensional subspace matches trained probe performance (0.90 AUC), enabling few-shot detection: on GPT-2, 25 labeled examples achieve 89% of full-data accuracy. We validate causally through activation steering: the learned direction produces 10.9 percentage point changes in error rates while random directions show no effect. Internal probes achieve 0.80-0.97 AUC; output-based methods (P(True), semantic entropy) achieve only 0.44-0.64 AUC. The correctness signal exists internally but is not expressed in outputs. That centroid distance matches probe performance indicates class separation is a mean shift, making detection geometric rather than learned.

papers.title: CLaS-Bench: A Cross-Lingual Alignment and Steering Benchmark
papers.research_question: How effective is steering for controlling output language compared to established approaches, and does it perform equally well across languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CLaS-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating multilingual steering, and finds that residual-based DiffMean steering consistently outperforms other methods.
papers.conclusion: CLaS-Bench provides a standardized benchmark for multilingual steering, enabling rigorous evaluation and revealing that simple residual-based methods are highly effective.
papers.key_findings:
DiffMean steering on residual activations consistently outperforms other methods, including prompting baselines.
Prompting exhibits failures for specific languages, while DiffMean succeeds across most languages.
Language-specific representations emerge predominantly in later layers (layers 16-32).
Steering directions cluster based on language family, indicating geometric structure in representation space.
papers.abstract: Understanding and controlling the behavior of large language models (LLMs) is an increasingly important topic in multilingual NLP. Beyond prompting or fine-tuning, , i.e.,~manipulating internal representations during inference, has emerged as a more efficient and interpretable technique for adapting models to a target language. Yet, no dedicated benchmarks or evaluation protocols exist to quantify the effectiveness of steering techniques. We introduce CLaS-Bench, a lightweight parallel-question benchmark for evaluating language-forcing behavior in LLMs across 32 languages, enabling systematic evaluation of multilingual steering methods. We evaluate a broad array of steering techniques, including residual-stream DiffMean interventions, probe-derived directions, language-specific neurons, PCA/LDA vectors, Sparse Autoencoders, and prompting baselines. Steering performance is measured along two axes: language control and semantic relevance, combined into a single harmonic-mean steering score. We find that across languages simple residual-based DiffMean method consistently outperforms all other methods. Moreover, a layer-wise analysis reveals that language-specific structure emerges predominantly in later layers and steering directions cluster based on language family. CLaS-Bench is the first standardized benchmark for multilingual steering, enabling both rigorous scientific analysis of language representations and practical evaluation of steering as a low-cost adaptation alternative.

papers.title: Transmuting prompts into weights
papers.research_question: Why do interventions like averaging contrastive activations or applying low-rank matrix updates succeed in controlling complex model behaviors? What is the underlying mathematical principle that connects a textual instruction to a specific change in a model’s weights or activations?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a theoretical foundation for activation steering and model editing by deriving a method to transmute prompts into reusable weight updates (thought vectors and matrices).
papers.conclusion: By bridging the gap between abstract transformer dynamics and tangible weight updates, this work provides a robust foundation for the next generation of efficient, mathematically grounded model editing techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Thought vectors and matrices can be derived from token patches via averaging and least-squares optimization.
This provides a theoretical explanation for heuristic activation steering (e.g., contrastive averaging) and low-rank model editing (e.g., ROME).
Empirical validation shows thought patches can specialize models for tasks like arithmetic, detoxification, translation, and knowledge retrieval, achieving performance comparable to full context prompting.
New knowledge can be integrated via thought patches, but performance degrades with dictionary size and query mismatch.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades with larger dictionary sizes and when retrieval queries differ from those used during patch computation, indicating overfitting to prompt structures.
future_direction: Developing more robust regularization schemes to prevent overfitting to prompt structures.
papers.abstract: A growing body of research has demonstrated that the behavior of large language models can be effectively controlled at inference time by directly modifying their internal states, either through vector additions to their activations or through updates to their weight matrices. These techniques, while powerful, are often guided by empirical heuristics, such as deriving steering vectors from the average activations of contrastive prompts. This work provides a theoretical foundation for these interventions, explaining how they emerge from the fundamental computations of the transformer architecture. Building on the recent finding that a prompt's influence can be mathematically mapped to token-dependent implicit weight updates (Dherin et. al, 2025), we derive a principled method for condensing this information into token-independent thought vectors and thought matrices. These constructs provide a theoretical explanation for existing vector-and-matrix-based model editing techniques and offer a direct, computationally-grounded method for transmuting textual input into reusable weight updates.

papers.title: Do Personality Traits Interfere? Geometric Limitations of Steering in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether personality steering directions are geometrically independent in large language models, what happens to steering effectiveness when geometric independence is explicitly enforced, and if observed trait dependencies are consistent across different model families.
papers.core_contribution: Personality steering directions in LLMs are not geometrically independent; enforcing orthogonality does not eliminate cross-trait behavioral effects and can reduce steering strength and fluency, indicating that traits occupy a coupled subspace.
papers.conclusion: Personality traits in large language models are not independent directions in activation space, and geometric constraints on steering vectors have limitations in achieving fully independent trait control.
papers.key_findings:
Personality steering directions exhibit substantial geometric dependence, with steering one trait inducing changes in others.
Enforcing geometric independence through hard orthonormalisation does not eliminate cross-trait effects and reduces fluency.
Cross-trait dependencies are consistent across different model families like LLaMA-3-8B and Mistral-8B.
Model-specific modulation exists, e.g., Neuroticism steering is strong in LLaMA-3 but weak in Mistral-8B.
Soft constraint methods like selective or soft projection offer a better trade-off between disentanglement and semantic preservation.
papers.limitation:
Limited to a small set of large language models and personality datasets.
Relies on linear geometric constraints; other orthogonalisation or projection methods are not explored.
Uses LLMs as judges for behavioral assessment without human evaluation.
future_direction: Extend analysis to a broader range of model families and trait representations.
Explore other orthogonalisation or projection methods beyond linear constraints.
Incorporate human evaluation or complementary metrics for assessment.
papers.abstract: Personality steering in large language models (LLMs) commonly relies on injecting trait-specific steering vectors, implicitly assuming that personality traits can be controlled independently. In this work, we examine whether this assumption holds by analysing the geometric relationships between Big Five personality steering directions. We study steering vectors extracted from two model families (LLaMA-3-8B and Mistral-8B) and apply a range of geometric conditioning schemes, from unconstrained directions to soft and hard orthonormalisation. Our results show that personality steering directions exhibit substantial geometric dependence: steering one trait consistently induces changes in others, even when linear overlap is explicitly removed. While hard orthonormalisation enforces geometric independence, it does not eliminate cross-trait behavioural effects and can reduce steering strength. These findings suggest that personality traits in LLMs occupy a slightly coupled subspace, limiting fully independent trait control.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal improve language model safety at inference time, and what are the trade-offs with general model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: SAE-based feature steering can improve refusal rates for unsafe prompts but introduces a systematic trade-off, degrading performance on safe prompts and general capability benchmarks, indicating deep entanglement between safety-relevant features and general language abilities.
papers.conclusion: While SAE-based feature steering is a promising, flexible approach for enhancing language model safety without retraining, its practical deployment is limited by significant trade-offs with general capabilities, highlighting the need to better understand and address feature entanglement.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal-mediating features can be identified using a simple, handcrafted prompt.
Amplifying identified SAE features (e.g., Feature 22373) increases refusal rates for unsafe prompts in both single-turn and multi-turn jailbreak settings.
This safety improvement comes with increased over-refusal on safe prompts.
Feature steering causes significant regression in factual recall (MMLU, TruthfulQA) and reasoning (GSM8K) performance, even on benign content.
Performance regressions are not unique to safety features; steering a non-safety feature (Feature 216 for philosophy) also degrades capabilities, suggesting a general limitation of the steering approach.
papers.limitation:
The feature identification method is not scalable, relying on a single handcrafted prompt.
Feature steering introduces a trade-off between improved safety and degraded performance on unrelated capabilities.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying features that mediate target behaviors.
Understanding why features are entangled with unrelated capabilities and how to isolate them.
Exploring conditional steering approaches that activate interventions only when needed.
papers.abstract: Responsible deployment of language models requires mechanisms for refusing unsafe prompts while preserving model performance. While most approaches modify model weights through additional training, we explore an alternative: steering model activations at inference time via amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal. This work uncovers a fundamental tension between SAE steering-based safety improvements and general model capabilities. While feature steering successfully improves robustness against both single-turn and challenging multi-turn jailbreak attempts, we discover that this comes at a previously underexplored cost -- systematic degradation of performance across multiple benchmark tasks, even on safe inputs with no apparent connection to refusal behavior. This suggests that features mediating refusal may be more deeply entangled with general language model capabilities than previously understood. Our findings reveal important open questions about the nature of safety-relevant features in language models and the feasibility of isolating them for targeted intervention. While SAE-based steering shows promise as a flexible approach to enhancing language model safety, our results highlight the critical need to understand and address the mechanisms behind these capability tradeoffs before such techniques can be practically deployed.

papers.title: Spherical Steering: Geometry-Aware Activation Rotation for Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we achieve effective inference-time control of language models without degrading their open-ended generation capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Spherical Steering, a training-free activation rotation method that improves multiple-choice accuracy and open-ended generation quality by preserving activation norms and using geometry-aware rotations.
papers.conclusion: Spherical Steering, a training-free activation steering method using geodesic rotation, consistently improves accuracy while enhancing open-ended generation quality, highlighting activation rotation as an effective primitive for inference-time control.
papers.key_findings:
Spherical Steering outperforms additive baselines (e.g., ITI, CAA) on multiple-choice benchmarks, improving average accuracy by over 8 points.
The method maintains or improves open-ended generation quality (TRUE×INFO) while boosting accuracy, unlike additive methods which degrade generation.
Norm-preserving rotation is more collapse-efficient than additive steering, achieving greater performance gains per unit of representational change.
The method is compatible with in-context learning, providing additional gains when combined with few-shot prompting.
The vMF confidence gate enables input-adaptive steering, improving selectivity and controllability.
future_direction: principled multi-layer layer selection
layer-adaptive calibration
papers.abstract: Inference-time steering has emerged as a promising paradigm for controlling language models (LMs) without the cost of retraining. However, standard approaches typically rely on activation addition, a geometric operation that inevitably alters the magnitude of hidden representations. This raises concerns about representation collapse and degradation of open-ended generation capabilities. In this work, we explore Spherical Steering, a training-free primitive that resolves this trade-off through activation rotation. Rather than shifting activations with a fixed vector, our method rotates them along a geodesic toward a target direction, guiding the activation toward the target concept while preserving the integrity of the signal. To further enhance adaptivity, we incorporate a confidence gate that dynamically modulates steering strength based on input uncertainty. Extensive experiments across multiple-choice benchmarks demonstrate that Spherical Steering significantly outperforms addition-based baselines (notably by +10% on TruthfulQA, COPA, and Storycloze), while simultaneously maintaining the model's general open-ended generation quality. This work highlights the value of geometric consistency, suggesting that norm-preserving rotation is a robust and effective primitive for precise inference-time control.

papers.title: Controllability Analysis of State Space-based Language Model
papers.research_question: Can the Influence Score, a controllability measure derived from control theory, serve as a diagnostic tool for interpreting, comparing, and understanding the internal dynamics of SSM-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper validates the Influence Score, a novel controllability measure derived from Mamba's state-space parameters, as a diagnostic tool for SSM-based language models, revealing scaling effects, architectural signatures, and emergent behaviors related to model capacity and robustness.
papers.conclusion: The Influence Score is a promising diagnostic tool for interpreting, comparing, and understanding the internal dynamics of SSM-based language models, revealing core architectural properties and emergent behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The Influence Score scales directly with model size and training data quality, serving as a proxy for model capacity.
Mamba exhibits consistent architectural signatures: a strong recency bias (position sensitivity) and a heavy concentration of influence in mid-to-late layers.
Emergent behaviors appear at scale: the largest model (mamba-2.8b-slimpj) intuitively ranks content words as more influential than function words and demonstrates robustness by decreasing internal influence when processing noisy inputs.
The Influence Score is largely insensitive to sampling temperature but increases systematically with prompt complexity.
The metric reveals a functional specialization across layers, with late layers showing significantly higher influence than early layers.
papers.limitation:
The Influence Score is an aggregated metric; future work should trace the influence of individual tokens or concepts through the network on a layer-by-layer basis.
The study was limited to three models; applying the framework to a wider range of SSMs and comparing to Transformers would be beneficial.
future_direction: Tracing the influence of individual tokens or concepts through the network on a layer-by-layer basis.
Applying the framework to a wider range of SSMs and comparing their influence fingerprints to traditional Transformers.
Using the Influence Score for guided generation, e.g., penalizing decoding paths that lead to unstable spikes in influence to improve model reliability.
papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs), particularly Mamba, have become powerful architectures for sequence modeling, yet their internal dynamics remain poorly understood compared to attention-based models. We introduce and validate the Influence Score, a controllability-based metric derived from the discretized state-space parameters of Mamba and computed through a backward recurrence analogous to system observability. The score quantifies how strongly a token at position k affects all later states and outputs. We evaluate this measure across three Mamba variants: mamba-130m, mamba-2.8b, and mamba-2.8b-slimpj, using six experiments that test its sensitivity to temperature, prompt complexity, token type, layer depth, token position, and input perturbations. The results show three main insights: (1) the Influence Score increases with model size and training data, reflecting model capacity; (2) Mamba exhibits consistent architectural patterns, including recency bias and concentrated influence in mid-to-late layers; and (3) emergent behaviors appear only at scale, with mamba-2.8b-slimpj uniquely prioritizing content words and reducing internal influence in the presence of noise. These findings establish the Influence Score as a practical diagnostic tool for interpreting and comparing SSM-based language models.

papers.title: Causal Language Control in Multilingual Transformers via Sparse Feature Steering
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoder (SAE) features be leveraged to steer the generated language of multilingual LLMs during inference without fine-tuning or explicit prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for causal language control in multilingual transformers by steering sparse autoencoder features, showing high success rates and layer-specific effectiveness.
papers.conclusion: Demonstrates that SAE features can be causally steered for controlled language shifts, revealing layer-localized sensitivity and architectural mechanisms like attention head specialization.
papers.key_findings:
Steering a single SAE feature can shift output language with up to 90% success while preserving semantic fidelity.
Language steering is most effective in mid-to-late transformer layers.
Specific attention heads, such as Head 12 in Layer 29, amplify language-sensitive SAE features.
Steering performance varies across layers and languages, with some layers showing localized attention contributions and others relying on inherited features.
The method outperforms prompt-based baselines in language classification accuracy for some languages.
papers.limitation:
All experiments are conducted exclusively on the Gemma model family, limiting generalizability to other architectures.
Identification of language-divergent SAE features relies on a fixed dataset of parallel sentences, which may not capture full diversity.
Evaluation depends on automatic metrics (FastText and LaBSE), which do not fully reflect human judgments of fluency or meaning preservation.
SAE features are derived from a pretrained sparse autoencoder and are not learned end-to-end for the steering task, limiting optimality.
Computational requirements are nontrivial for inference and scaling to larger models.
future_direction: Generalizing the framework to non-language attributes (e.g., tone, dialect)
Extending interpretability analysis to MLP contributions and other model families
papers.abstract: Deterministically controlling the target generation language of large multilingual language models (LLMs) remains a fundamental challenge, particularly in zero-shot settings where neither explicit language prompts nor fine-tuning are available. In this work, we investigate whether sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, previously shown to correlate with interpretable model behaviors, can be leveraged to steer the generated language of LLMs during inference. Leveraging pretrained SAEs on the residual streams of Gemma-2B and Gemma-9B, we identify features whose activations differ most significantly between English and four target languages: Chinese, Japanese, Spanish, and French. By modifying just a single SAE feature at one transformer layer, we achieve controlled language shifts with up to 90\% success, as measured by FastText language classification, while preserving semantic fidelity according to LaBSE (Language-Agnostic BERT Sentence Embedding) similarity. Our analysis reveals that language steering is most effective in mid-to-late transformer layers and is amplified by specific attention heads disproportionately associated with language-sensitive SAE features. These results demonstrate the promise of sparse feature steering as a lightweight and interpretable mechanism for controllable multilingual generation.

papers.title: ExpertLens: Activation steering features are highly interpretable
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether the features discovered by activation steering methods in large language models are interpretable, and if they align with human representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ExpertLens, a method based on activation steering, and shows that the expert neurons it identifies are stable across models and datasets, and their representations align closely with human conceptual structures.
papers.conclusion: ExpertLens is a flexible and lightweight approach for interpretability of LLMs, providing insights into model representations that align with human concepts.
papers.key_findings:
ExpertLens representations are stable across models and datasets.
ExpertLens representations align closely with human representations, matching inter-human alignment levels.
ExpertLens significantly outperforms the alignment captured by word/sentence embeddings.
ExpertLens can reconstruct human conceptual structure (domain organization).
Experts are learned from data, with larger models having more experts.
papers.limitation:
Only single-word concepts are considered.
Do not have access to training data.
Model choice (Pythia family).
Study neurons individually.
Polysemantic neurons are discussed.
future_direction: Future work will consider more complex concepts such as those expressing human values or preferences.
Exploration of alignment and its emergence in alternative model families.
Studying neurons jointly to capture additional aspects of concept representation.
papers.abstract: Activation steering methods in large language models (LLMs) have emerged as an effective way to perform targeted updates to enhance generated language without requiring large amounts of adaptation data. We ask whether the features discovered by activation steering methods are interpretable. We identify neurons responsible for specific concepts (e.g., ``cat'') using the ``finding experts'' method from research on activation steering and show that the ExpertLens, i.e., inspection of these neurons provides insights about model representation. We find that ExpertLens representations are stable across models and datasets and closely align with human representations inferred from behavioral data, matching inter-human alignment levels. ExpertLens significantly outperforms the alignment captured by word/sentence embeddings. By reconstructing human concept organization through ExpertLens, we show that it enables a granular view of LLM concept representation. Our findings suggest that ExpertLens is a flexible and lightweight approach for capturing and analyzing model representations.

papers.title: The Representation and Recall of Interwoven Structured Knowledge in LLMs: A Geometric and Layered Analysis
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode interwoven scientific knowledge, and do they reflect geometric structures like the periodic table?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode scientific knowledge in geometric structures, such as a 3D spiral aligning with the periodic table, representing knowledge as interwoven manifolds rather than isolated facts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop internal representations that reflect the structured geometry of scientific knowledge, representing symbolic knowledge as geometry-aware, interwoven manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure is observed in hidden states that aligns with the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous attributes enabling indirect recall, while deeper layers sharpen categorical distinctions.
Linguistic context increasingly shapes representations in later layers.
Middle layers have strong linear associations between related attributes, which weaken in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Prompts are focused on chemical elements and may not extend to domains with more abstract features.
Hypothesis-driven validation may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge, such as materials property prediction.
Informing the design of downstream embedding-based tasks.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how large language models (LLMs) represent and recall multi-associated attributes across transformer layers. We show that intermediate layers encode factual knowledge by superimposing related attributes in overlapping spaces, along with effective recall even when attributes are not explicitly prompted. In contrast, later layers refine linguistic patterns and progressively separate attribute representations, optimizing task-specific outputs while appropriately narrowing attribute recall. We identify diverse encoding patterns including, for the first time, the observation of 3D spiral structures when exploring information related to the periodic table of elements. Our findings reveal a dynamic transition in attribute representations across layers, contributing to mechanistic interpretability and providing insights for understanding how LLMs handle complex, interrelated knowledge.

papers.title: Style Vectors for Steering Generative Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can style vectors derived from layer activations be used to steer the output of large language models towards specific styles such as sentiment, emotion, or writing style?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that style vectors can be computed from layer activations to steer LLM outputs towards desired styles, providing a more nuanced and controllable approach compared to prompt engineering.
papers.conclusion: Style vectors enable continuous and adjustable modulation of LLM outputs, with activation-based vectors being the preferred method due to their efficiency and performance.
papers.key_findings:
Activation-based style vectors are more resource-efficient and perform better than training-based vectors.
Steering is more effective for subjective prompts than for factual prompts.
Layers 18, 19, and 20 are most effective for style encoding and steering.
The parameter λ allows continuous control of steering strength but can lead to nonsensical outputs if set too high.
Style vectors can successfully steer outputs towards sentiments, emotions, and writing styles.
papers.limitation:
High computational cost for deriving trained steering vectors, requiring sample length restrictions.
Reliance on existing sentiment and emotion classifiers for evaluation, which may not be perfect.
Experiments focus on English text only, limiting generalizability to other languages.
future_direction: Determining the exact influence of the weighting parameter λ for different domains.
Conducting studies on human perceptions of steered text styles.
Investigating style steering for languages other than English and more complex styles.
papers.abstract: This research explores strategies for steering the output of large language models (LLMs) towards specific styles, such as sentiment, emotion, or writing style, by adding style vectors to the activations of hidden layers during text generation. We show that style vectors can be simply computed from recorded layer activations for input texts in a specific style in contrast to more complex training-based approaches. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of activation engineering using such style vectors to influence the style of generated text in a nuanced and parameterisable way, distinguishing it from prompt engineering. The presented research constitutes a significant step towards developing more adaptive and effective AI-empowered interactive systems.

papers.title: Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness of Language Models
papers.research_question: Can language models internally distinguish between testing and deployment phases (evaluation awareness), and how can this capability be probed and steered?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that evaluation awareness is linearly represented in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and can be extracted using linear probes, and that steering with evaluation-awareness-relevant SAE features can partially uncover sandbagging behavior.
papers.conclusion: Modern language models develop internal representations that distinguish evaluation from deployment contexts; current evaluation scenarios may be readily identifiable as artificial, highlighting the need for more realistic evaluation frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes trained on model activations can detect evaluation contexts with high AUROC scores (up to 0.829).
The probes generalize across different evaluation and deployment prompt datasets.
Current safety evaluation prompts (e.g., for deception) are often classified as test-like, suggesting models may recognize them as artificial evaluations.
Steering with SAE features related to evaluation awareness can partially recover sandbagged capabilities on the WMDP benchmark, but linear probe steering had minimal impact.
Evaluation awareness representations are more distinctly encoded in earlier model layers (e.g., layers 23-24).
papers.limitation:
The evaluation awareness observed in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct may be less pronounced than in frontier models, raising concerns about generalizability.
Linear probes may not capture the full complexity of evaluation awareness, which may not be strictly one-dimensionally linear.
The experimental setup is a significant simplification compared to real-world scenarios of concern (e.g., extended agentic backdoor honeypots).
Steering attempts using linear probes and SAE features showed limited success in modifying sandbagging behavior.
future_direction: Comprehensive red-teaming with alternative probe training methods (e.g., logistic regression, PCA, non-linear probes).
Leveraging probes to enhance the realism of scheming honeypots via automated prompt authenticity enhancement.
Integrating probe-based detection into control protocols as a low-latency whitebox monitoring system.
papers.abstract: Language models can distinguish between testing and deployment phases -- a capability known as evaluation awareness. This has significant safety and policy implications, potentially undermining the reliability of evaluations that are central to AI governance frameworks and voluntary industry commitments. In this paper, we study evaluation awareness in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. We show that linear probes can separate real-world evaluation and deployment prompts, suggesting that current models internally represent this distinction. We also find that current safety evaluations are correctly classified by the probes, suggesting that they already appear artificial or inauthentic to models. Our findings underscore the importance of ensuring trustworthy evaluations and understanding deceptive capabilities. More broadly, our work showcases how model internals may be leveraged to support blackbox methods in safety audits, especially for future models more competent at evaluation awareness and deception.

papers.title: Trust Me, I'm an Expert: Decoding and Steering Authority Bias in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Investigates whether language models exhibit systematic bias based on the perceived expertise of endorsement sources, and how source expertise influences model behavior across domains.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that LLMs exhibit hierarchical authority bias, becoming more susceptible to incorrect endorsements from higher-expertise sources, and shows that this bias can be reduced by steering the model's residual stream.
papers.conclusion: LLMs prioritize source credibility over semantic correctness, making them vulnerable to authority bias, but this bias can be mechanistically isolated and controlled via steering vectors.
papers.key_findings:
Models show progressively larger accuracy gains with correct endorsements as source expertise increases.
High-expertise incorrect endorsements induce confident errors, with models becoming more confident in wrong answers.
Reasoning models remain susceptible to expert endorsement despite chain-of-thought capabilities.
Mathematical reasoning tasks show lower robustness rates (largest susceptibility), while medical tasks show higher resistance.
Authority bias can be mechanistically reduced by subtracting a steering vector extracted from the residual stream.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are constrained to smaller open-source models (up to 32B parameters); frontier-scale models may exhibit different patterns of authority susceptibility.
Evaluation only covers four domains (mathematical, legal, and medical reasoning); broader domain coverage would strengthen generalization claims.
Endorsement format is limited to single, explicit answer statements without variations in phrasing, confidence levels, or reasoning justification.
Have not yet conducted comprehensive analysis across layers or utilized interpretability methods like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to fully characterize the underlying representations.
future_direction: larger-scale evaluations
richer interaction scenarios
deeper mechanistic investigations
papers.abstract: Prior research demonstrates that performance of language models on reasoning tasks can be influenced by suggestions, hints and endorsements. However, the influence of endorsement source credibility remains underexplored. We investigate whether language models exhibit systematic bias based on the perceived expertise of the provider of the endorsement. Across 4 datasets spanning mathematical, legal, and medical reasoning, we evaluate 11 models using personas representing four expertise levels per domain. Our results reveal that models are increasingly susceptible to incorrect/misleading endorsements as source expertise increases, with higher-authority sources inducing not only accuracy degradation but also increased confidence in wrong answers. We also show that this authority bias is mechanistically encoded within the model and a model can be steered away from the bias, thereby improving its performance even when an expert gives a misleading endorsement.

papers.title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for "Quirky" Language Models
papers.research_question: Can internal model features be used to detect anomalous training signals (when models use faulty heuristics) in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Mechanistic anomaly detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks but are not effective across all models and tasks; MAD may be effective in low-stakes applications but requires advances for high-stakes settings.
papers.conclusion: Anomaly detection results are inconsistent across models and tasks; while sometimes highly discriminative, performance degrades to chance in some cases, indicating that more work is needed for reliable real-world application.
papers.key_findings:
Anomaly detector performance varies significantly between models (model-dependent detection).
Detection efficacy is strongly task-dependent (e.g., arithmetic tasks yield higher performance).
Larger deviations in behavior generally make anomalies easier to detect, though not universally.
Anomaly detection performance is closely related to the linear separability of features between normal and anomalous classes.
Detectors that depend on different features (activations vs. attribution) offer somewhat independent signals, but naive combination did not improve performance.
papers.limitation: The manipulations in the datasets are artificial, and real-world tasks will differ systematically, likely with systematic changes in detector performance.
future_direction: Conduct additional experiments to assess whether models trained on more tokens make anomaly detection harder.
Develop benchmarks more closely aligned with intended real-world tasks.
Advances in both detection and evaluation are needed for high-stakes settings.
papers.abstract: As LLMs grow in capability, the task of supervising LLMs becomes more challenging. Supervision failures can occur if LLMs are sensitive to factors that supervisors are unaware of. We investigate Mechanistic Anomaly Detection (MAD) as a technique to augment supervision of capable models; we use internal model features to identify anomalous training signals so they can be investigated or discarded. We train detectors to flag points from the test environment that differ substantially from the training environment, and experiment with a large variety of detector features and scoring rules to detect anomalies in a set of ``quirky'' language models. We find that detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks, but no detector is effective across all models and tasks. MAD techniques may be effective in low-stakes applications, but advances in both detection and evaluation are likely needed if they are to be used in high stakes settings.

papers.title: Identifiable Steering via Sparse Autoencoding of Multi-Concept Shifts
papers.research_question: How can we provably recover interpretable concepts from LLM activations in an unsupervised manner, ensuring identifiability to avoid entangled representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Shift Autoencoders (SSAEs), a method that learns sparse representations of differences between embeddings, provably recovering steering vectors for individual concepts from paired observations with multiple unknown concept shifts, under identifiability guarantees.
papers.conclusion: SSAEs offer a provably identifiable approach for unsupervised concept recovery and steering in LLMs, advancing interpretability by ensuring learned representations correspond to genuine underlying concepts.
papers.key_findings:
SSAEs achieve identifiability up to permutation and scaling under assumptions of linear representation and sufficient diversity of multi-concept shifts.
Empirically, SSAEs outperform standard sparse autoencoders and other baselines in Mean Correlation Coefficient (MCC) across synthetic and real-world language datasets.
SSAEs provide more accurate steering, as measured by cosine similarity between steered and target embeddings, especially when concepts are correlated.
SSAE steering vectors generalize better out-of-distribution compared to non-identifiable methods.
The method successfully recovers concepts in real-world tasks such as bias mitigation, truthfulness, sycophancy, and refusal.
papers.limitation:
The identifiability guarantees rely on assumptions such as the Linear Representation Hypothesis and sufficient diversity of multi-concept shifts, which may not hold in all practical settings.
The theoretical analysis assumes the encoder dimension is known (equal to the number of varying concepts |V|), but in practice this is often unknown and a larger dimension is used, which can affect identifiability.
future_direction: Extending the method to non-linear representations.
Applying the approach to other modalities beyond text.
Scaling the method to larger models and more complex datasets.
papers.abstract: Steering methods manipulate the representations of large language models (LLMs) to induce responses that have desired properties, e.g., truthfulness, offering a promising approach for LLM alignment without the need for fine-tuning. Traditionally, steering has relied on supervision, such as from contrastive pairs of prompts that vary in a single target concept, which is costly to obtain and limits the speed of steering research. An appealing alternative is to use unsupervised approaches such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to map LLM embeddings to sparse representations that capture human-interpretable concepts. However, without further assumptions, SAEs may not be identifiable: they could learn latent dimensions that entangle multiple concepts, leading to unintentional steering of unrelated properties. We introduce Sparse Shift Autoencoders (SSAEs) that instead map the differences between embeddings to sparse representations. Crucially, we show that SSAEs are identifiable from paired observations that vary in \textit{multiple unknown concepts}, leading to accurate steering of single concepts without the need for supervision. We empirically demonstrate accurate steering across semi-synthetic and real-world language datasets using Llama-3.1 embeddings.

papers.title: ContextFocus: Activation Steering for Contextual Faithfulness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be used to improve contextual faithfulness in LLMs when external context conflicts with internal knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ContextFocus, an activation steering method that improves contextual faithfulness in LLMs under knowledge conflicts without fine-tuning and with minimal inference overhead.
papers.conclusion: ContextFocus is an effective activation steering method that improves contextual faithfulness in RAG systems, offering a practical and scalable solution without fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
ContextFocus improves contextual faithfulness across QA, MR, and MC subsets of ConFiQA, increasing ps and decreasing po and MR.
ContextFocus complements prompting strategies like O&I, yielding further improvements when combined.
ContextFocus remains effective on larger models such as Llama-3.1-70B.
Steering vectors are data-efficient, with performance saturating after 1.5k training examples.
Jointly contrasting system instruction and contextual evidence is critical for effective steering, outperforming isolated contrasts.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation focuses on question-answering under knowledge-conflict settings, not covering open-ended or long-form generation tasks.
Fixed steering multiplier across all inputs; adaptive control could be beneficial.
future_direction: Extending activation-level steering to open-ended or long-form generation tasks.
Developing adaptive or input-conditional control of steering strength.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode vast amounts of parametric knowledge during pre-training. As world knowledge evolves, effective deployment increasingly depends on their ability to faithfully follow externally retrieved context. When such evidence conflicts with the model's internal knowledge, LLMs often default to memorized facts, producing unfaithful outputs. In this work, we introduce ContextFocus, a lightweight activation steering approach that improves context faithfulness in such knowledge-conflict settings while preserving fluency and efficiency. Unlike prior approaches, our solution requires no model finetuning and incurs minimal inference-time overhead, making it highly efficient. We evaluate ContextFocus on the ConFiQA benchmark, comparing it against strong baselines including ContextDPO, COIECD, and prompting-based methods. Furthermore, we show that our method is complementary to prompting strategies and remains effective on larger models. Extensive experiments show that ContextFocus significantly improves contextual-faithfulness. Our results highlight the effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency of ContextFocus in improving contextual-faithfulness of LLM outputs.

papers.title: Towards Inference-time Category-wise Safety Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we steer LLM generations to safety using gradient-free, inference-time steering methods? The paper explores category-specific steering vectors and sophisticated extraction methods for safety steering.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a category-specific inference-time safety steering method for LLMs that uses steering vectors computed from harmful and harmless activations, with unsupervised and guided extraction methods and pruning to improve steering performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates effective category-specific inference-time safety steering for LLMs using activation-based steering vectors, providing best practices and highlighting trade-offs between safety and text quality.
papers.key_findings:
Category-specific steering reduces unsafe responses, with varying effectiveness across harm categories and models.
Pruning activations based on L2 norms improves safety steering and can retain or improve text quality.
Using generic harmless data (e.g., Alpaca Instructions) for steering vectors can be effective, reducing the need for category-specific harmless data.
Guided activations (filtered by an external safety classifier) can further reduce unsafe responses but may degrade text quality.
The method works better for Llama3-8B than Llama2-7B, and there is a trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.limitation:
Only attention activations were used for steering; other activation types (MLP, residual stream, block outputs) were not explored.
A simple pruning method based on L2 norms was used; more sophisticated pruning could be explored.
The method does not optimize for text quality, leading to potential degradation in helpfulness and coherence.
future_direction: Explore other types of activations or combinations for steering.
Develop better pruning methods to obtain cleaner steering signals.
Add constraints to the steered generation to improve the trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have seen unprecedented advancements in capabilities and applications across a variety of use-cases, safety alignment of these models is still an area of active research. The fragile nature of LLMs, even models that have undergone extensive alignment and safety training regimes, warrants additional safety steering steps via training-free, inference-time methods. While recent work in the area of mechanistic interpretability has investigated how activations in latent representation spaces may encode concepts, and thereafter performed representation engineering to induce such concepts in LLM outputs, the applicability of such for safety is relatively under-explored. Unlike recent inference-time safety steering works, in this paper we explore safety steering of LLM outputs using: (i) category-specific steering vectors, thereby enabling fine-grained control over the steering, and (ii) sophisticated methods for extracting informative steering vectors for more effective safety steering while retaining quality of the generated text. We demonstrate our exploration on multiple LLMs and datasets, and showcase the effectiveness of the proposed steering method, along with a discussion on the implications and best practices.

papers.title: Automated Neuron Labelling Enables Generative Steering and Interpretability in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we automatically label neurons in protein language models with natural language descriptions, and how can these labels be used to steer protein generation towards desired properties?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an automated neuron labeling framework for protein language models and a neuron activation-guided steering method to generate proteins with desired biochemical and structural properties.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a framework for automated neuron labeling and generative steering in protein language models, enabling interpretability and control over protein generation, and suggests future directions for integration with structural validation and model pruning.
papers.key_findings:
Automated neuron labeling produces interpretable descriptions that capture diverse biochemical and structural properties of proteins.
Neuron activation-guided steering can generate proteins with targeted characteristics, such as specific molecular weight, GRAVY score, and secondary/tertiary structural motifs.
Larger PLMs capture more fine-grained protein features and show a more distributed representation of features across layers compared to smaller models.
Feature encoding follows a hierarchical pattern: sequence-derived properties peak in early layers, structural properties in middle layers, and functional properties in later layers.
Negative steering (multiplying neuron activations by negative values) can invert the effect for some features (e.g., GRAVY score) but not for others (e.g., instability index).
papers.limitation:
LLM explainer may generate oversimplified or hallucinated descriptions.
Generated proteins may not fold into viable, stable structures due to high ΔG values.
Limited to three models due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Incorporate a reinforcement learning module with structure prediction models (e.g., AlphaFold2) to improve structural viability of generated proteins.
Extend neuron labeling to more models and use multiple LLMs for more robust labels.
Explore pruning neurons based on labels to compress models while retaining performance.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) encode rich biological information, yet their internal neuron representations are poorly understood. We introduce the first automated framework for labeling every neuron in a PLM with biologically grounded natural language descriptions. Unlike prior approaches relying on sparse autoencoders or manual annotation, our method scales to hundreds of thousands of neurons, revealing individual neurons are selectively sensitive to diverse biochemical and structural properties. We then develop a novel neuron activation-guided steering method to generate proteins with desired traits, enabling convergence to target biochemical properties like molecular weight and instability index as well as secondary and tertiary structural motifs, including alpha helices and canonical Zinc Fingers. We finally show that analysis of labeled neurons in different model sizes reveals PLM scaling laws and a structured neuron space distribution.

papers.title: Refusal in LLMs is an Affine Function
papers.research_question: How can affine concept editing (ACE) provide more precise and standardized control over refusal behavior in language models compared to existing steering methods?
papers.core_contribution: ACE unifies directional ablation and activation addition in an affine framework, enabling more standardized and precise control over refusal behavior in language models, and generalizes to models where prior methods fail.
papers.conclusion: ACE offers a more consistent and standardized approach for steering refusal behavior in LLMs, mitigating limitations of existing methods and working across diverse model architectures.
papers.key_findings:
ACE provides more standardized steering than contrastive activation addition (CAA), reducing dependency on input prompts for refusal control.
ACE corrects the issue of nonsense generation in models like Hermes Eagle RWKV v5, where directional ablation alone produces incoherent outputs.
The standardization effect of ACE is not perfect, but parameters slightly below zero and above one are effective for controlling refusal.
ACE works on both transformer-based models (e.g., Llama 3) and recurrent neural networks (e.g., RWKV v5), demonstrating generalizability.
ACE combines affine subspace projection and activation addition to reliably control refusal across different prompt types.
papers.limitation: The standardization effect of ACE is not perfect, suggesting that steering vectors may be flawed or that directional ablation does not fully erase information.
future_direction: Exploring whether nonlinear techniques are required to fully erase concepts like refusal.
Extending steering techniques to work reliably on a more varied set of behaviors.
papers.abstract: We propose affine concept editing (ACE) as an approach for steering language models' behavior by intervening directly in activations. We begin with an affine decomposition of model activation vectors and show that prior methods for steering model behavior correspond to subsets of terms of this decomposition. We then provide a derivation of ACE and use it to control refusal behavior on ten different models, including Llama 3 70B. ACE combines affine subspace projection and activation addition to reliably control the model's refusal responses across prompt types. We evaluate the results using LLM-based scoring on a collection of harmful and harmless prompts. Our experiments demonstrate that ACE consistently achieves more precise control over model behavior than existing methods and generalizes to models where directional ablation via affine subspace projection alone produces incoherent outputs. Code for reproducing our results is available at https://github.com/EleutherAI/steering-llama3 .

papers.title: Beyond Prompt Engineering: Robust Behavior Control in LLMs via Steering Target Atoms
papers.research_question: How can we achieve precise control over language model generation by isolating and manipulating disentangled knowledge components (target atoms) using sparse autoencoders?
